feedbackItems.pattern: AdjacencyList lazy iterator regression from SCC refactor
feedbackItems.explanation: This test (along with testSuccessorIteratorIsLazy) verifies that the AdjacencyList predecessor and successor iterators do not eagerly build a collection on construction, instead computing elements on demand. The iterator was first implemented in run 46, where the successor iterator stored a local copy of the adjacency list. In run 53, the implementation was refactored to avoid storing the list reference, instead re-querying keyToVertex.get(KEY).successors on each hasNext() and next() call. This change was repeated in run 54 with the same pattern. The test then experienced a regression at run 115, where changes to the Graph class replaced predecessorSet/successorSet calls with HashSet-based queue tracking for the SCC implementation. The SCC code path called predecessorSet() or successorSet(), which triggered eager set construction during what should have been a laziness timing test. Run 116 applied the same Graph.java fix, and by run 117 both lazy iteration tests passed. The core issue was that the SCC implementation in the shared Graph superclass was calling eager neighbor-set methods, and the laziness test measured construction time of the iterator, which was affected by the eager set calls happening in the same graph instance or test setup.
nextSteps: This lazy-iterator pattern recurs in the Final practice computer part, where successorIterator is called inside an inner loop and an eager implementation will time out. To ensure laziness, your iterator's constructor should do O(1) work: store only the starting index or reference, and advance to the first valid element only when hasNext() or next() is called.

When implementing graph algorithms in a shared superclass (like Graph.java), prefer using iterators (successorIterator/predecessorIterator) over set-returning methods (successorSet/predecessorSet) for traversal. Calling successorSet inside BFS forces O(degree) eager work per vertex, which defeats laziness guarantees and adds unnecessary overhead.

Test lazy iteration yourself by timing only the constructor and first hasNext() call. If your iterator pre-computes all neighbors, that timing will scale with vertex count; a truly lazy iterator will return in constant time regardless of graph size.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

feedbackItems.pattern: BFS shortest path rewritten from recursive to iterative with path reconstruction fixes
feedbackItems.explanation: This test (along with testAMShortestPathExampleGraphs) validates BFS-based shortest path returning a List of vertices from start to end, or an empty list if unreachable. The test first failed at run 48 when Milestone 1 was complete but Milestone 2 methods returned null. Run 69 added handling for the empty-paths case, wrapping the result extraction in an emptiness check, which was the first passing run. Run 72 then performed a major rewrite, replacing the recursive shortestPathHelper with an iterative BFS using a Queue and Stack of Token objects plus a visited HashMap, which is the standard BFS-with-parent-map approach. However, this rewrite introduced regressions. Run 83 rewrote the path reconstruction logic, replacing the recursive pathMaker with a Token-based while loop that traces back through the visited map, but used reference equality (!=) instead of .equals() for comparing startLabel and endLabel. Run 84 refined this further by changing a null-check to a containsValue check. Run 87 shows another iteration of the same path reconstruction fix. The test required multiple attempts across 35 total failing runs because the path reconstruction from the BFS parent map involves several error-prone steps: off-by-one errors in whether start and end vertices are included, incorrect termination conditions in the backtracking loop, and reference vs. value equality all contributed to repeated failures before final stabilization.
nextSteps: This BFS shortest-path pattern is the canonical Final graph-programming question, using the same signature and BFS-with-parent-map approach. To solidify the technique: run BFS from start, storing parent[neighbor] = current for each discovered neighbor, stop when you dequeue end, then reconstruct the path by following parent pointers from end back to start and reversing.

Always use .equals() rather than == when comparing generic keys of type T. Reference equality fails for Integer values above 127 and for any non-interned String, which causes subtle bugs in path reconstruction that only appear on certain inputs.

Handle the edge cases explicitly at the top of shortestPath: if start.equals(end), return a single-element list; if end is never reached during BFS, return an empty list. Separating these cases from the main BFS logic prevents the backtracking loop from producing incorrect results.

drills.intro: The Final's graph programming section often asks for a BFS-flavored method that's related to shortestPath but not identical — practice that pattern by implementing public int countReachableWithinKHops(T from, int k) on your Graph<T> (or in AdjacencyListGraph if you prefer): it returns the count of vertices reachable from `from` using at most k directed edges, including `from` itself at hop 0. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone2ALTest.java. Note: that file's existing @Test methods route through Core helpers and don't import assertEquals directly — add `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;` at the top before the test compiles.
hints: Standard BFS with explicit hop tracking: keep a Queue of (vertex, distance) pairs and a HashSet of visited vertices. Pop one at a time, skip if already visited, mark visited, count it. Push successors (via successorIterator) only when their distance is ≤ k.

Off-by-one trap: countReachableWithinKHops(start, 0) returns 1 — the start vertex itself counts at distance 0. countReachableWithinKHops(start, 1) returns 1 plus the number of distinct direct successors. The hop count is the number of edges traversed, not the number of vertices visited.

Don't call successorSet inside the BFS inner loop — it eagerly builds a HashSet per call. Use successorIterator for O(1) construction. Eager construction blows an O(V+E) BFS up to O(V·E) or worse, which is exactly what the Final's perf-bound version of this question is designed to catch.

feedbackItems.pattern: AdjacencyMatrix predecessor iterator hasNext logic rewritten twice
feedbackItems.explanation: This test verifies that the AdjacencyMatrix predecessor iterator correctly traverses all vertices that have an edge pointing to the given vertex. The test failed from run 1 through run 23 as the AdjacencyMatrix implementation was built incrementally. Run 24 introduced the PredecessorIterator inner class with the initial implementation, scanning columns of the adjacency matrix to find predecessors, and the test first passed. However, a regression occurred later, and run 107 shows a significant rewrite of the hasNext() and next() methods. The original hasNext() simply checked whether the index was within bounds (index < matrix.length), but this is incorrect for a predecessor iterator because not every row in the column contains an edge. The fix in run 107 restructured hasNext() to advance the index past non-edge entries, returning false when the index exceeds matrix.length, and returning true only when positioned at an actual edge. The next() method was similarly updated. A matrix-based predecessor iterator must scan forward through the column to find the next row where matrix[row][col] is true, and hasNext() must perform this scan without consuming the element, while next() must return the element and advance past it.
nextSteps: For the Final's graph problem, iterator correctness is critical since successorIterator is called in inner loops. For a matrix-based iterator, hasNext() should advance an internal index to the next true entry in the relevant row or column, caching that position so next() can return it without re-scanning. This 'advance-on-hasNext, return-on-next' pattern avoids both skipping elements and returning non-edges.

When implementing hasNext() for a sparse structure like an adjacency matrix column, the method must do real work: skip over false entries until it finds a true one or exhausts the array. A simple bounds check (index < length) is insufficient because most entries may be false. Consider writing a private advance() helper that both hasNext() and next() delegate to.

Test your iterator with graphs that have gaps: vertices with no incoming edges interspersed with vertices that do have incoming edges. This exercises the scanning logic and catches off-by-one errors in the index advancement.

The triple (A, B, C) and (B, C, A) and (C, A, B) describe the same triangle (a 3-cycle has three rotations). One way to count each triangle exactly once is to enforce a fixed ordering on the triple — e.g. require u to compare-less-than both v and w using vertex.toString().

If you're seeing 6 where the test expects 2, you're counting each triangle three times (once per rotation). Either divide by 3 at the end, or restrict to one canonical rotation per triangle as described above.

feedbackItems.pattern: SCC two-pass BFS required eager-set elimination for scalability
feedbackItems.explanation: This test (along with testALStronglyConnectedComponentExampleGraphs) validates that stronglyConnectedComponent returns the set of all vertices mutually reachable from a given key via the intersection of forward and reverse BFS reachability sets. The test first failed at run 48 when the stub returned null. Run 91 commented out the stub overrides in both AdjacencyListGraph and AdjacencyMatrixGraph, allowing the shared Graph superclass implementation to take effect, and the test first passed. However, a critical regression occurred around run 111 where the SCC implementation returned only single-vertex sets instead of full components. Run 112 fixed this by replacing the predecessorSet/successorSet calls with explicit HashSet-based BFS traversal using a queueSet to track visited vertices. The before-code shows the SCC method calling predecessorSet(key) and successorSet(key) to seed the reachability computation, but these eager set methods only return immediate neighbors, not the full transitive closure. The after-code introduces a proper BFS loop that maintains a queueSet of all discovered vertices, adding each newly discovered neighbor to both the BFS queue and the queueSet, ensuring the full reachable set is computed. This fix also resolved the wiki_surfing timeout because predecessorSet on the 460k-vertex graph was O(V) per call, and calling it repeatedly during BFS made the SCC computation quadratic.
nextSteps: The 2023 Final's findUnknownBalloons question builds directly on stronglyConnectedComponent. The correct SCC algorithm performs two BFS passes: one following successor edges to find all forward-reachable vertices, one following predecessor edges to find all reverse-reachable vertices, then intersects the two sets. Make sure each BFS computes full transitive reachability, not just immediate neighbors.

When implementing BFS for reachability, maintain a visited set (or 'queueSet') that is checked before enqueuing any vertex. This prevents re-processing vertices and ensures O(V+E) time. Without this check, the same vertex can be enqueued multiple times, leading to quadratic behavior on dense graphs.

Distinguish between neighbor methods (successorSet returns immediate neighbors) and reachability methods (BFS from a vertex returns all transitively reachable vertices). SCC requires the latter; using the former produces only the 1-hop neighborhood, which is why the regression returned single-vertex components.

drills.intro: Your Milestone 2 stronglyConnectedComponent returns the SCC containing one specific key. The Final practice's graph section often asks for a related-but-different question: 'is the entire graph one big SCC?' Practice it by implementing public boolean isStronglyConnected() on your Graph<T> that returns true iff every vertex can reach every other vertex. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone2AMTest.java. As with the BFS drill, you'll need to add `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;` and `import java.util.HashSet;` at the top — neither is currently in M2ALTest's import block.
hints: Algorithm: pick any vertex v from keySet(). Do a forward BFS from v (via successorIterator) — collect every vertex it reaches. Do a reverse BFS from v (via predecessorIterator) — collect every vertex that reaches it. The graph is strongly connected iff both reachable sets equal keySet().

Why one vertex is sufficient: if v reaches everyone (forward) and everyone reaches v (reverse), then for any pair a, b, the path a → v → b exists (concatenate reverse-of-a-to-v with forward-of-v-to-b). You don't have to check V·V pairs separately.

Edge case: a single-vertex graph is trivially strongly connected — its lone vertex reaches itself with the zero-length path. Your BFS will visit only the start vertex, the reachable set is {v}, keySet() is {v}, and the comparison naturally returns true. If your code special-cases size 1 to false, you've added a bug.

feedbackItems.pattern: Wiki-scale SCC timeout fixed by eliminating eager set calls in BFS
feedbackItems.explanation: This wiki_surfing integration test runs stronglyConnectedComponent on the 460k-vertex Wikipedia living-people graph, requiring both correctness and performance. The test failed from run 49 through run 111, a span of 63 runs. Initially (runs 49-52), the SCC method returned null because Milestone 2 was unimplemented. After the SCC algorithm was implemented around run 91, the test continued to fail due to timeout on the large graph. The root cause was that the SCC implementation called predecessorSet() and successorSet() during its BFS traversal. These methods eagerly construct a Set of all neighbors, and when called repeatedly inside a BFS loop on a 460k-vertex graph, the cumulative cost became quadratic. Run 112 replaced these eager set calls with an explicit BFS loop that maintains a HashSet (queueSet) of visited vertices, adding each discovered neighbor to both the queue and the visited set. This change reduced the SCC computation from O(V * average_degree) repeated set constructions to a single O(V+E) BFS pass in each direction, bringing the total runtime within the test's timeout. The fix simultaneously resolved the correctness regression from run 111 (where SCC returned only single vertices) because the new BFS loop properly computes full transitive reachability rather than just immediate neighbors.
nextSteps: The WikiSurfing spec notes that failures usually trace back to a Milestone 1 method that is correct on small examples but quadratic on large graphs. When writing graph algorithms, always use iterators (successorIterator/predecessorIterator) for traversal rather than set-returning methods. Iterators allow O(1) per-element access without constructing an intermediate collection, which is critical for O(V+E) BFS on large graphs.

For the Final's graph question, the same O(V+E) performance discipline applies. Structure your BFS with three components: a Queue for the frontier, a Set for visited vertices (checked before enqueuing), and iterator-based neighbor traversal. This pattern guarantees each vertex and edge is processed exactly once.

When debugging timeout issues on large graphs, profile by counting method calls rather than wall-clock time. If predecessorSet() is called V times during a BFS, each constructing a set of size up to V, the total work is O(V^2), which explains the timeout on 460k vertices.

drills.intro: Your SCC works, but the key lesson was avoiding eager set copies inside BFS loops. Let's reinforce that: add a countReachable(T start) method to your graph that returns the number of vertices reachable from start (including start itself) using BFS, and make sure it runs in O(V+E) time. Paste the test into GraphSurfingMilestone2TestCore.java for a point back.
hints: Hint 1: countReachable is just BFS from start, counting every vertex you visit. The critical constraint is that you never call a method that copies an entire neighbor set into a new collection inside the loop.

Hint 2: Use a Queue<T> and a HashSet<T> for visited. On each dequeue, iterate over successors using your lazy iterator (successorIterator), not successorSet(). Increment a counter for each newly-visited vertex.

Hint 3: Inside your graph class, add: public int countReachable(T start) { Set<T> visited = new HashSet<>(); Queue<T> q = new LinkedList<>(); visited.add(start); q.add(start); while (!q.isEmpty()) { T cur = q.poll(); Iterator<T> it = successorIterator(cur); while (it.hasNext()) { T nb = it.next(); if (visited.add(nb)) q.add(nb); } } return visited.size(); }

feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testAddAndRawStringNoCollision, testAddAndRawStringNoRehash, testAddDuplicate, testAddAll, testClear, testRemove, and testContains, first passed at run 4 when the Node class fields (data, next), the backing array, size counter, and capacity field were properly declared and initialized. These tests then regressed at run 11 when a large code change introducing rehash logic and restructuring the add method left a syntax error (a missing closing brace after the contains-check guard clause in add). The diff at run 11 shows the contains guard was rewritten from a multi-line if-block to a single-line form, and the rehash threshold check and full rehash() method were added, but the brace mismatch prevented compilation. At run 12, the same logical changes were applied with corrected syntax, restoring all of these tests to passing. The core issue was that a large batch of new code (rehash, capacity doubling, reinsert logic) was added in a single step without verifying that the existing add method's control flow remained syntactically valid.
nextSteps: When adding a major feature like rehash() that modifies the add method's control flow, make smaller incremental changes: first refactor the add method's structure, verify existing tests still pass, then add the rehash call and method body separately.

Practice the load-factor threshold check independently: the condition (size + 1 > loadFactor * capacity) must be evaluated before inserting the new element, and rehash must redistribute every existing node by recomputing its bucket index against the new capacity.

For separate chaining, ensure that after rehash the new array is fully initialized to null buckets and that each node is re-inserted at the head of its new chain, not simply copied by reference from the old array.

drills.intro: Let's stretch your understanding of size tracking: implement a countCollisions() method that returns how many elements share a bucket with at least one other element. Paste this test into StringHashSetTest.java and it is worth a point back.
hints: Hint 1: A collision means a bucket's linked list has more than one node. countCollisions counts every element in such buckets, not the number of buckets.
Hint 2: Iterate over each bucket in the internal array. For each bucket, walk the chain and count its length. If the length is >= 2, add that length to your running total.
Hint 3: In your loop, for each non-null bucket head, follow .next pointers to count nodes. If count >= 2, add count to the result. Return the result after visiting all buckets.

feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testIteratorNextHasNext, testIteratorConcurrentModificationException, and testIteratorNoSuchElementException, failed across all 13 runs from run 1 through run 13 because the iterator was not implemented. The iterator() method originally returned null, causing NullPointerException in early runs, and no iterator inner class existed. At run 14, a substantial 123-line addition implemented the complete iterator: a modCount field was added to StringHashSet and incremented on every mutation (add, remove, clear), the iterator inner class was created with state tracking for the current bucket index and current node within a chain, hasNext() was implemented to scan forward across buckets to find the next non-null entry, next() was implemented to return the current element and advance, and both NoSuchElementException (when next() is called past the end) and ConcurrentModificationException (when the collection is mutated during iteration) were properly thrown by comparing an expectedModCount snapshot against the live modCount. The iterator for a separate-chaining hash set is notably more complex than a simple linked-list iterator because it must traverse two dimensions: across array buckets and along each bucket's chain. This java.util.Iterator contract pattern recurs in EditorTrees, graphs, and every mutable collection you will write; mastering the hasNext/next/exception protocol here builds a foundation for those future implementations.
nextSteps: The modCount/expectedModCount pattern for fail-fast iterators recurs in every mutable collection you will build, including EditorTrees and graph structures. For iterating over a separate-chaining hash table, the key technique is maintaining two pieces of state: the current bucket index and the current node pointer within that bucket's chain. When the chain is exhausted (node becomes null), advance the bucket index until a non-null bucket is found or the array is fully scanned.
Practice writing next() so it saves the return value before advancing the internal pointer. A common bug is advancing first and then returning, which skips the first element or returns the wrong one.

feedbackItems.pattern: Deferred implementation resolved in single batch
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed for 13 consecutive runs because no iterator implementation existed; the iterator() method returned null. At run 14, the full iterator inner class was added, including the ConcurrentModificationException detection mechanism. The implementation introduced a modCount field on StringHashSet that is incremented on every structural modification (add, remove, clear). The iterator captures this value as expectedModCount at construction time and checks it at the beginning of hasNext() and next(). If the values diverge, meaning the collection was mutated after the iterator was created, a ConcurrentModificationException is thrown. This is the standard fail-fast iterator pattern from java.util.AbstractList and HashMap. The ConcurrentModificationException/fail-fast pattern recurs in every mutable collection you will implement; understanding that it is a structural safeguard (not a concurrency lock) is important for future work.
nextSteps: The ConcurrentModificationException pattern is structural, not a one-off fix. Ensure every method that changes the hash set's logical contents (add, remove, clear, and rehash if it changes size) increments modCount. Rehash alone, if it only redistributes without changing size, may or may not need to increment modCount depending on your design, but add/remove/clear always must.

When testing your own CME logic, verify that creating an iterator, then calling add() or remove() on the set, then calling iterator.next() throws the exception. Also verify that calling hasNext() after mutation throws it, since some implementations only check in next().

Remember that the expectedModCount is set once at iterator construction. If you create a new iterator after a mutation, it should work fine with the updated modCount; only pre-existing iterators should throw.

feedbackItems.pattern: Deferred implementation resolved in single batch
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed for 13 runs because the iterator() method returned null, so any call to hasNext() or next() produced a NullPointerException. At run 14, the complete iterator was implemented with proper bucket-and-chain traversal logic. The hasNext() method must scan forward from the current position (current node in the current bucket, then subsequent buckets) to determine if any elements remain. The next() method must return the current element's data, then advance the internal pointer: first to the next node in the chain, and if that chain is exhausted, to the first non-null entry in a subsequent bucket. This two-level traversal is the defining challenge of iterating over a separate-chaining hash table. The java.util.Iterator contract (hasNext/next/NoSuchElementException) recurs in every collection you build, including EditorTrees and graph traversals.
nextSteps: To iterate a separate-chaining hash set correctly, initialize the iterator by scanning from bucket 0 to find the first non-null entry. Store both the bucket index and the node pointer. In next(), save the current node's data, advance to node.next, and if node.next is null, scan forward through buckets to find the next chain head.

Ensure hasNext() is idempotent: calling it multiple times without calling next() should always return the same result and should not advance any internal state. A common mistake is advancing the bucket index inside hasNext(), which causes elements to be skipped.

Test your iterator on edge cases: an empty set (hasNext returns false immediately), a set where all elements hash to the same bucket (single chain traversal), and a set with elements spread across many buckets (multi-bucket traversal).

When next() is called and hasNext() would return false, meaning all buckets and chains have been exhausted, the iterator must throw NoSuchElementException rather than returning null or causing a NullPointerException. Distinguish between NoSuchElementException (thrown when iteration is exhausted) and ConcurrentModificationException (thrown when the collection is mutated). In next(), check for concurrent modification first, then check for exhaustion, so the error messages are accurate.

feedbackItems.pattern: Null return from incomplete iterator implementation
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 1 through 5 before passing at run 6. The initial runs (1-2) involved building out core BST methods like contains, size, and height, followed by toArrayList in run 2. At that point the inefficient iterator compiled but returned null instead of the expected values, indicating that toArrayList was not yet correctly populating the list or the iterator was not properly wrapping it. Runs 4 and 5 addressed regressions and added toString, respectively, but the inefficient iterator remained broken. By run 6, the underlying toArrayList method was working correctly, which allowed the inefficient iterator (which depends on converting the tree to an ArrayList and then iterating over that list) to return valid results. The core issue was that the inefficientIterator method depends entirely on a correct toArrayList implementation, so until that in-order traversal logic was complete, the iterator could not function.
nextSteps: This in-order traversal pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString(), which must run in O(N) via in-order traversal; practice writing recursive in-order traversal that populates a collection, ensuring the base case (NULL_NODE) returns without adding anything and the recursive case visits left, processes current, then visits right.

Understand the dependency chain: inefficientIterator delegates to toArrayList, which delegates to a recursive helper. When debugging a method that wraps another, verify the inner method independently first by checking its output on a small tree before testing the outer method.

Compare the inefficient iterator approach (build entire ArrayList up front, then iterate) with the lazy stack-based iterator to understand the time/space tradeoffs; the inefficient version is O(n) space and O(n) construction time, while the stack-based version is O(h) space with O(1) amortized next().

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect recursive pointer reassignment in remove
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testRemove, failed across runs 82-87. The initial remove implementation at run 82 had two core issues: (1) the recursive delete calls did not reassign the return value back to the left/right child pointer (e.g., `right.delete(element, bc)` instead of `right = right.delete(element, bc)`), and (2) the predecessor's subtree was incorrectly reattached using `this.left.right = predecessor.left` instead of `this.left = predecessor.left`. Run 83 introduced a NullPointerException. By run 87, the fix changed the recursive calls to `left = left.delete(element, bc)` and `right = right.delete(element, bc)`, and fixed the predecessor reattachment to `this.left = predecessor.left`. In a BST remove using the NULL_NODE sentinel pattern, every recursive call must return the (possibly updated) subtree root, and the parent must capture that return value to maintain correct tree structure.
nextSteps: This pointer-replacement-on-return pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) uses the same three-case removal logic but adds AVL rebalancing on the way back up. Practice writing remove so that every recursive call returns the new subtree root and the caller always reassigns: left = left.delete(...), right = right.delete(...).

Review the two-children removal case carefully: after finding the in-order predecessor, you must copy its data into the current node, then recursively delete the predecessor's value from the left subtree. The left subtree pointer must be updated with the result of that recursive deletion.

Test remove with trees of varying shapes: a left-only chain, a right-only chain, a balanced tree, and cases where the node to remove is the root. Each exercises a different combination of the leaf, one-child, and two-children cases.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect stack push targets and hasNext logic in pre-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 11-41 before passing at run 42. The error progression shows: initially hasNext() returned true when it should have returned false (run 11), then returned false when it should have returned true (run 14), then the iterator produced extra elements (run 15, expected 5 but got 6). The root cause across these runs involved two issues. First, the next() method was pushing the node itself (`stack.push(n)`) back onto the stack instead of pushing its children (`stack.push(n.right)` and `stack.push(n.left)`), which caused incorrect traversal. Second, the hasNext() method toggled between `!stack.isEmpty()` and `stack.peek() != NULL_NODE`, with the correct solution combining both checks: `!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() != NULL_NODE`. The fix at run 42 changed the push targets to `n.right` and `n.left` (pushing right first so left is processed first), wrapped next() in a try-catch for proper exception handling, and switched hasNext() to use the peek-based check.
nextSteps: The pre-order traversal pattern, where you process the current node then push right-child-first and left-child-second, is foundational for EditorTrees toString() and for exam questions requiring you to predict traversal output from a given tree. Practice implementing all three iterative traversals (pre, in, post) using an explicit stack to solidify the push order for each.

For hasNext() with a NULL_NODE sentinel, always guard against both an empty stack and a NULL_NODE on top. The combined check `!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() != NULL_NODE` prevents EmptyStackException while correctly detecting traversal completion.
When debugging iterator issues, trace through a small tree (3-5 nodes) by hand, writing out the stack contents after each next() call. This makes push-target errors immediately visible.

feedbackItems.pattern: EmptyStackException evolving to NoSuchElementException in in-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 49-73, with the error evolving from EmptyStackException to NoSuchElementException. The in-order iterator is more complex than pre-order because you cannot simply pop-and-process; you must first descend to the leftmost node before returning any value. The initial EmptyStackException (run 49) indicates the stack was being emptied prematurely, likely because the iterator was popping without properly pushing successors. The shift to NoSuchElementException (run 51) indicates the hasNext()/next() interaction was adjusted but the traversal logic still did not correctly handle moving to the in-order successor. The fix at run 74 shows a significant restructuring: the old approach tried to peek at the left child of the top-of-stack and manage a complex conditional, while the corrected version simplified to popping a node, then pushing its right child and left descendants. The hasNext() was also corrected from `return true` (which caused infinite iteration) to `!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() != NULL_NODE`.
nextSteps: The in-order iterator pattern directly parallels EditorTrees toString(), which must perform an O(N) in-order traversal. The standard stack-based in-order algorithm is: (1) in the constructor, push all left-spine nodes; (2) in next(), pop a node, record its value, then push the right child followed by all of that child's left descendants. Master this pattern as it recurs throughout the course.

When hasNext() unconditionally returns true, the iterator will never terminate, causing tests to hang or throw exceptions when the stack empties during next(). Always tie hasNext() to actual stack state, not a hardcoded value.

Trace the in-order iterator on a 5-node balanced BST by hand: write out the stack after the constructor, then after each next() call. Verify that elements come out in sorted order and that the stack is empty exactly when all nodes have been visited.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incomplete two-children removal case with missing subtree cleanup
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 82-94, persisting longer than the simpler testRemove and testRemoveReturnValue tests. While those tests passed by runs 85 and 87 respectively, testRemoveAdvanced continued to fail because it exercises more complex removal scenarios, particularly the two-children case where the in-order predecessor must be found, its data copied to the current node, and then the predecessor must be recursively deleted from the left subtree. The code diff at run 95 shows the critical fix: adding `left = left.delete(data, bc)` in the two-children case and adding `return this` to ensure the current node is properly returned after modification. Earlier attempts (visible in the testRemoveReturnValue diffs at runs 87-93) show different approaches to predecessor cleanup: directly reassigning `this.left`, setting `predecessor = predecessor.left`, and commenting out lines. The correct approach, implemented at run 95, is to copy the predecessor's data into the current node, then recursively call delete on the left subtree to remove the predecessor node, capturing the result back into the left pointer.
nextSteps: The two-children removal algorithm is: (1) find the in-order predecessor by going left once then right as far as possible, (2) copy the predecessor's data into the node being removed, (3) recursively delete the predecessor's key from the left subtree with `left = left.delete(predecessorData, bc)`. This same logic applies in EditorTrees Milestone 3 with the added complexity of maintaining balance codes.

The `return this` statement after modifying a node during removal is essential; without it, the parent loses its reference to the modified subtree. Every branch of the delete method must return either the current node (if it was modified in place) or a replacement node (if the current node was removed).

Test the two-children case specifically with trees where the predecessor has a left child of its own. This is the scenario that breaks naive implementations that simply unlink the predecessor without recursively cleaning up its subtree.

feedbackItems.pattern: StackOverflowError from broken iterator bucket traversal
feedbackItems.explanation: The toString test failed across all 8 runs (runs 1-8) before passing in run 9. The test threw a StackOverflowError, which originated in the iterator's advance-to-next-element logic. The original code contained a contradictory condition: `if(currentNode.next == null)` as an outer check, followed by `if(currentNode.next != null)` inside it, making the inner branch unreachable. Additionally, `currentBucket++` appeared twice without proper null guards, causing the iterator to skip buckets or fail to terminate. In run 9, the fix restructured the logic to check `currentNode != null && currentNode.next != null` for chain traversal within a bucket, and separately handled bucket increment with a null guard on `currentNode`. This eliminated the infinite loop and allowed toString to correctly iterate and format all elements.
nextSteps: When writing iterator advance logic for a hash table, always handle two distinct transitions separately: (1) moving to the next node within the same bucket's chain, and (2) moving to the first node of the next non-empty bucket. Mixing these into nested conditionals with contradictory guards is a common source of infinite loops.

Before dereferencing any node reference (e.g., currentNode.next), always check that the reference itself is non-null. This defensive null-checking pattern prevents NullPointerException and is especially important in sparse data structures like hash tables where many buckets are null.

When toString depends on an iterator, test the iterator independently first. If the iterator has a bug like an infinite loop, toString will amplify it into a StackOverflowError, making the root cause harder to diagnose.

diffs.label: Run 9 — StringHashSet.java
diffs.note: Restructured the iterator's advance method to separate chain traversal (currentNode.next) from bucket advancement (currentBucket++), adding null guards on currentNode that eliminated the infinite loop causing StackOverflowError in toString.

feedbackItems.pattern: NullPointerException from unguarded node dereference in iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testIteratorNextHasNext, testIteratorConcurrentModificationException, and testIteratorNoSuchElementException, all failed for 8 consecutive runs (runs 1-8) due to the same bug in the iterator's bucket traversal logic. The iterator was first attempted in run 3, but the advance logic contained a critical flaw: the outer condition `if(currentNode.next == null)` would enter a block that then checked `if(currentNode.next != null)`, a logically impossible branch, so the chain-following code was unreachable. Meanwhile, `currentBucket++` was called unconditionally and duplicated, causing the iterator to skip past valid buckets or dereference null nodes. This produced NullPointerException when the iterator tried to access `currentNode.next` on a null reference, and the broken traversal also caused the StackOverflowError seen in toString. Runs 3 through 8 showed no change in test outcomes, indicating the same flawed logic persisted. In run 9, the fix added a proper null guard (`currentNode != null && currentNode.next != null`) for chain traversal and conditionally incremented `currentBucket` only when `currentNode` was non-null, correctly separating intra-bucket and inter-bucket movement. This resolved all four iterator-related tests simultaneously.
nextSteps: The java.util.Iterator contract (hasNext/next/NoSuchElementException) recurs in every collection you implement, including EditorTrees and graphs. Practice writing the advance logic as a clear state machine: after returning a value, first try to follow the chain in the current bucket; if exhausted, scan forward through buckets until a non-null head is found or the table ends.

The ConcurrentModificationException / fail-fast iterator pattern using modCount and expectedModCount is structural and reappears in every mutable collection. Make sure your iterator captures expectedModCount at construction time and checks it at the start of every next() call, independent of the traversal logic.

When multiple tests fail with the same stack trace pointing to the same method, focus debugging effort on that single method rather than trying to fix tests individually. In this case, all five failures traced back to the same advance/next logic in the iterator.

feedbackItems.pattern: Iterator hasNext() crash on empty stack
feedbackItems.explanation: This pre-order iterator test failed from Run 2 through Run 22, requiring 21 failed runs before passing at Run 23. Early runs showed the method was undefined, then NullPointerExceptions appeared as stub implementations returned null, and later runs produced assertion failures as the iterator logic produced incorrect results. The fix at Run 23 addresses a critical issue: the hasNext() method was calling stack.peek() without first checking whether the stack was empty. The diff shows an added guard (if(!stack.isEmpty())) wrapping the peek-based NULL_NODE check. Calling hasNext() after exhausting all elements would throw an EmptyStackException or produce incorrect results without this guard. Pre-order traversal visits root, then left, then right, and the stack-based implementation must handle the termination condition cleanly when no nodes remain to visit.
nextSteps: This traversal pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString(), which requires O(N) in-order traversal; practice writing stack-based iterators where you always guard stack operations (peek, pop) with an isEmpty() check before accessing elements.

Review the three traversal orders (pre-order, in-order, post-order) and how each maps to a stack-based iterator. Pre-order pushes right then left so that left is processed first; make sure your hasNext() correctly detects when the stack is fully drained versus when it contains only NULL_NODE sentinels.
Write a small test that creates an iterator on a single-node tree and calls hasNext()/next() until exhaustion, then calls hasNext() one more time. This edge case catches missing empty-stack guards.

drills.intro: The Final's graph programming section asks you to extend Graph<T> with a new traversal method on top of your Milestone 1 work. Practice that exact pattern by adding a public int numDirectedTriangles() method to your Graph<T> (or its AL/AM subclasses) that returns the number of directed 3-cycles in the graph — that is, ordered triples of distinct vertices (u, v, w) with edges u→v, v→w, w→u. Then paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java for a self-check. The simple 3-vertex case is the warm-up; harder variants follow.
hints: A directed triangle (u, v, w) requires three directed edges: u→v, v→w, and w→u. The simplest correct implementation iterates over all ordered triples of distinct vertices and checks the three edges via hasEdge — but it must not double-count.

The triple (A, B, C) and (B, C, A) and (C, A, B) describe the same triangle (a 3-cycle has three rotations). One way to count each triangle exactly once is to enforce a fixed ordering on the triple — e.g. require u to compare-less-than both v and w using vertex.toString().

If you're seeing 6 where the test expects 2, you're counting each triangle three times (once per rotation). Either divide by 3 at the end, or restrict to one canonical rotation per triangle as described above.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method as the warm-up, now on a 6-vertex example from the Final practice's computer part. The graph below has exactly 3 directed triangles after all 9 edges are added. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java after the simple case passes. If your count is wildly off, the bug is usually rotation-double-counting; if it's off by one or two, you may be misreading the edge list — sketch the adjacency list on paper first.
hints: Build the adjacency list on paper before running. From A: A→B. From B: B→C, B→D. From C: C→A, C→E, C→F. From D: D→E. From E: E→B, E→F. From F: nothing. With those edges in hand, scan for closed 3-cycles by inspection — that gives you the answer to compare against your code.

If you're seeing 9 instead of 3, you're counting each of the three triangles three times (one per rotation). If you're seeing 6 or 18, you're counting both rotations AND reflections — but in a directed graph there is no reflection symmetry, so check your loop bounds.

A reliable iteration shape: for u in keySet(), for v in successorSet(u), for w in successorSet(v) — if hasEdge(w, u) and {u,v,w} are pairwise distinct, increment. Then divide the running count by 3 once at the end.

feedbackItems.pattern: Eager predecessor iterator took nine runs to make lazy
feedbackItems.explanation: This lazy_iteration test failed across runs 1 through 9. Runs 1-2 failed due to null pointer exceptions in the underlying graph methods. By run 4, the predecessor iterator was functionally correct but delegated to predecessorSet(key).iterator(), which builds a full Set of predecessors upfront. The laziness test checks that constructing the iterator and calling next() once completes within a tight time bound on a large graph, which fails with eager Set construction. The successor lazy test was fixed at run 5 with a dedicated inner class, but the predecessor side was not addressed until run 10. The run 10 diff shows the removal of "return predecessorSet(key).iterator()" and its replacement with a PredecessorIterator inner class that stores a column index and scans rows on demand. This approach for an adjacency matrix achieves O(1) construction and O(1) per next() call by checking single cells rather than building a full Set.
nextSteps: This lazy-iteration concept recurs in the Final practice computer section; internalize that for an adjacency matrix, a lazy predecessor iterator holds a column index and a row cursor, advancing through matrix[row][col] on each next() call rather than collecting all predecessors into a Set at construction time.

When you have a working eager implementation and need to make it lazy, the key insight is to move the loop that scans for neighbors out of the constructor and into hasNext()/next(), maintaining a cursor that remembers where the scan left off between calls.

Verify laziness yourself before running the test: if your iterator's constructor calls any method that iterates over all vertices (like predecessorSet), it is not lazy regardless of whether it returns correct results.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

feedbackItems.pattern: AdjacencyList predecessorSet returned null across three runs
feedbackItems.explanation: This neighbor_sets test failed across runs 12-14 during the AdjacencyList implementation phase. At run 12, the initial AL implementation had most methods unimplemented, and predecessorSet was among the 11 failing tests. By run 13, 9 additional tests passed (including iterators and degree methods), but both successorSet and predecessorSet still returned null. Run 14 fixed successorSet but not predecessorSet. The test passed at run 15. In an adjacency list representation, predecessorSet requires iterating over all vertices and checking whether the current vertex appears in each vertex's successor list, which differs from successorSet (which returns the adjacency list for the given vertex directly). The staggered fix across runs 14 and 15 corresponds to separate implementations of successorSet and predecessorSet.
nextSteps: BFS and DFS trace tables on the Final paper section list the successor set at each step; ensure you understand that in an adjacency list, successorSet is O(1) lookup of the neighbor list, while predecessorSet requires O(V) traversal of all adjacency lists to find which vertices have an edge pointing to the query vertex.

Consider whether your AdjacencyList stores a separate reverse-adjacency map (predecessor lists) alongside the forward-adjacency map; maintaining both at insertion time makes predecessorSet O(1) lookup instead of O(V), which matters for algorithms like BFS that call it repeatedly.

When implementing paired methods like successorSet and predecessorSet, implement and test them together to catch asymmetries early; returning null instead of an empty Set for a vertex with no predecessors is a distinct bug from not implementing the method at all.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect stack element type and traversal logic in pre-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across 11 runs (runs 18 through 28). The initial failure at run 18 returned null instead of the expected value 6, indicating the iterator's traversal logic was incomplete. By run 19, the error shifted to hasNext() incorrectly returning true when it should return false, which persisted unchanged through runs 20, 21, and 22. The root cause, visible in the run 29 diff, was twofold: the stack was storing data values (Stack<T>) instead of nodes (Stack<Node>), and the hasNext() method was checking node references (root != NULL_NODE || root.left != NULL_NODE || root.right != NULL_NODE) instead of simply checking whether the stack was empty. The fix changed the stack type to Stack<Node>, pushed the root node during initialization only if it was not NULL_NODE, rewrote hasNext() to return !stck.isEmpty(), and restructured next() to pop a node and push its right then left children. This correctly implements the standard stack-based pre-order traversal pattern.
nextSteps: The stack-based pre-order traversal pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString(), which requires O(N) in-order traversal; internalize the general approach of pushing nodes (not data) onto a stack and letting the stack drive hasNext() so you can adapt it to any traversal order.

Practice converting between pre-order, in-order, and post-order stack-based iterators by hand: pre-order pushes right then left after popping, while in-order pushes all left descendants first. Understanding these differences will help with HW6's preOrderInOrderBuild problem.

When implementing any iterator, keep the invariant simple: hasNext() should check one condition (e.g., stack emptiness), and next() should be the only method that modifies state. Avoid duplicating traversal logic between the two methods.

diffs.label: Run 29 — BinarySearchTree.java
before: return root != NULL_NODE || root.left != NULL_NODE || root.right != NULL_NODE;
after: Node node = stck.pop();  // visit this node
// push right first so left is popped/peeked first (LIFO)
diffs.note: Changed stack type from Stack<T> to Stack<Node>, rewrote hasNext() to check stack emptiness instead of node references, and restructured next() to push children nodes, fixing the pre-order traversal logic.

feedbackItems.pattern: Null iterator return followed by incorrect hasNext() state management
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across 9 runs (runs 30 through 38). The initial failure at run 30 was a NullPointerException when calling hasNext(), indicating the iterator method was returning null rather than an iterator object. Runs 31 through 33 showed the iterator still returning null. By run 34, the error changed to hasNext() returning true when false was expected, mirroring the same state-management bug seen in the pre-order iterator. The in-order iterator requires a different initialization strategy than pre-order: rather than just pushing the root, it must push all left-spine nodes onto the stack so that the smallest element is on top. The test was ultimately fixed at run 39, likely by correctly initializing the stack with the leftmost path and, in next(), pushing the right child's left spine after popping.
nextSteps: The in-order iterator pattern directly parallels EditorTrees toString(), which must traverse nodes in rank order at O(N). Master the technique: initialize by pushing all nodes along the left spine, then on each next() call, pop a node, and if it has a right child, push that child's entire left spine.

Compare your pre-order and in-order iterators side by side to solidify the difference: pre-order processes a node immediately upon popping and pushes right then left; in-order defers processing until all left descendants are stacked. This distinction is tested on Exam 3.
When an iterator returns null or throws NullPointerException, verify that the iterator() method in the outer class actually instantiates and returns the iterator object, not null.

feedbackItems.pattern: Confused Node vs. data parameter in recursive insert causing NullPointerException
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testInsertReturnValueString() and testInsertStrings() failed across runs 11 through 13 due to the same underlying bugs in the insert method. At run 11, a NullPointerException occurred because the insert helper received a Node object but compared it against NULL_NODE (a sentinel node, not null), and the constructor call new Node(node.data) was fragile when node references were confused. Run 12 fixed the null pointer issue but left ordering broken. Run 13 fixed integer ordering but strings still failed, likely because compareTo() was being checked against the literal value 1 instead of using < 0 and > 0. The run 14 diff shows the comprehensive fix: the method signature changed from accepting a Node parameter to accepting raw data (T ndata), the base case changed from checking node == NULL_NODE to this == NULL_NODE (correctly detecting when recursion has reached a leaf position), and the comparison logic was corrected. This eliminated the confusion between the node being inserted and the current node in the tree.
nextSteps: The recursive descent-and-return pattern used here (where each recursive call returns the updated subtree root) recurs in EditorTrees add(char, int); practice writing insert helpers where the parameter is the data to insert and 'this' is the current tree node, returning the possibly-new subtree root.
Always use compareTo() with < 0, == 0, and > 0 rather than checking for specific values like 1 or -1. The Comparable contract only guarantees the sign of the return value, not its magnitude.

When designing recursive Node methods, keep a clear distinction between the data being passed down (the value to insert) and the structural context (the current node, accessed via 'this'). Mixing these two concepts is a common source of NullPointerExceptions in tree code.

drills.intro: Add sproutToDepth(int d) to BinarySearchTree.java so that every null child slot of any pre-existing node at depth < d is replaced with a new node whose value equals its parent's value. Only existing nodes are visited — newly sprouted nodes do not themselves sprout children. Special case: calling sproutToDepth(0) on an empty tree creates a root with value 0. This is a 2020-21 practice Exam 2 question combining full-tree structural modification with a depth parameter. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: Write a recursive helper sproutHelper(node, currentDepth, targetDepth): if node is NULL_NODE or currentDepth >= targetDepth, return immediately — there is nothing to sprout.

At each existing node, check the left child: if it is NULL_NODE, create new BinaryNode(node.data) and assign it (do NOT recurse into it); if it is not NULL_NODE, recurse into it with currentDepth+1. Do the same for right.
The public method handles the empty-tree special case: if targetDepth >= 0 and root == NULL_NODE, set root = new BinaryNode(0). Otherwise call sproutHelper(root, 0, targetDepth).

feedbackItems.pattern: Multiple pointer-update bugs in remove helper across all three cases
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed at runs 42 and 43 as part of a group of 3 failing remove tests. The run 44 diff reveals five distinct bugs that were fixed simultaneously. First, the outer remove call was not reassigning root (root.remove(...) instead of root = root.remove(...)), so removing the root node had no effect on the tree. Second, the one-child case returned 'this' instead of 'right' when the left child was NULL_NODE, failing to bypass the removed node. Third, the two-children case called searchLeft(root) instead of searchLeft(left), searching the wrong subtree for the in-order predecessor. Fourth, the subsequent removal of the predecessor was performed on the right subtree instead of the left. Fifth, the searchLeft helper traversed left (node = node.left) instead of right (node = node.right), so it found the minimum of the left subtree rather than the maximum (the actual in-order predecessor). All five fixes were necessary together to make remove work correctly.
nextSteps: The three-case remove logic (leaf, one child, two children with in-order predecessor/successor swap) recurs directly in EditorTrees Milestone 3 delete(int pos), which adds AVL rebalancing on top. Solidify your understanding of which subtree to search and which child pointer to update during the swap-and-delete step.

Practice the pointer-replacement pattern: every recursive remove helper must return the updated subtree root so the parent can reassign its child pointer. Forgetting root = root.remove(...) at the top level is equivalent to forgetting left = left.remove(...) in the recursive case; both silently discard the structural change.

When using the in-order predecessor approach (largest value in the left subtree), the search helper must go right repeatedly from the left child. Conversely, in-order successor means going left repeatedly from the right child. Draw a small tree and trace both approaches to confirm your implementation matches.

diffs.note: Fixed five bugs in remove: reassigned root from remove call, returned correct child in one-child case, searched correct subtree for predecessor, removed predecessor from correct subtree, and fixed searchLeft to traverse right instead of left.

The core issue across both test runs was ensuring that the recursive remove helper correctly returns the updated subtree reference at every level of recursion, and that the boolean 'was removed' signal propagates back to the caller without being overwritten by the newly added null checks.

feedbackItems.pattern: Missing root reassignment in recursive remove
feedbackItems.explanation: testRemoveReturnValue() and testRemove() both failed from run 13 through run 19 and were fixed at run 20, requiring 7 runs. The run 20 diff shows two key changes. First, `root.remove(element, bC)` was updated to `root = root.remove(element, bC)`, and similarly for insert. When remove() returns a new subtree root (for example, after deleting the root node itself), the tree's root field must be reassigned to capture this return value; otherwise, the root field continues pointing to the old, now-detached node. Second, the two-children removal case was modified: the predecessor's left child was being unconditionally reassigned, but the fix added a guard (`if (left != predecessor)`) to handle the edge case where the in-order predecessor is the immediate left child. The change from `if` to `else if` in the comparison chain also corrected a logic error where multiple branches could execute for the same node, causing incorrect tree structure after removal.
nextSteps: This pointer-replacement pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) uses the same three-case removal logic but must also rebalance; practice writing remove so that every recursive call returns the (possibly new) subtree root and the caller always reassigns its child pointer to that returned value.

For the two-children case in BST removal, trace through the scenario where the in-order predecessor is the direct left child versus a deeper right-descendant. The guard condition on predecessor reassignment prevents accidentally detaching the left subtree when the predecessor has no right children.

Use `else if` chains (not independent `if` statements) when the comparison outcomes are mutually exclusive. Independent `if` blocks can cause a node that was just identified as equal to also fall into the greater-than or less-than branch if data changes mid-method.

feedbackItems.pattern: Missing ConcurrentModificationException for addAll mutation
feedbackItems.explanation: This test has failed across all 14 runs, making it the only remaining failing test in the implementation. The test checks that mutating the hash set during iteration throws a ConcurrentModificationException (CME). The standard fail-fast pattern requires a modCount field on the collection that is incremented on every structural modification (add, remove, clear, addAll), and an expectedModCount field in the iterator that is set to modCount at construction time. On each call to hasNext() or next(), the iterator compares expectedModCount to modCount and throws CME if they differ. The run 13 diff shows the iterator tracks expectedSize and throws CME when expectedSize != size, but this approach has a limitation: the addAll() method likely increments size by the same amount as the number of elements added, yet if it does not also trigger the CME detection mechanism properly, or if the check only runs in next() but not in the right place, the test will miss the mutation. Additionally, using size comparison instead of a dedicated modCount can fail when an addAll followed by a remove leaves size unchanged, making the pattern fundamentally fragile. Across all 14 runs, the addAll() method has not been connected to the modification-tracking mechanism.
nextSteps: The modCount/expectedModCount pattern recurs in every mutable collection you will write, including EditorTrees and graph structures. Replace your size-based comparison with a dedicated modCount integer field: increment modCount in every method that structurally modifies the set (add, remove, clear, and addAll). In your iterator constructor, capture expectedModCount = modCount, then check expectedModCount != modCount at the start of both hasNext() and next().

Verify that addAll() increments modCount for each successful insertion, or at minimum once if any insertion occurs. The key insight is that addAll delegates to add(), so if add() already increments modCount, addAll will naturally trigger CME detection without extra code.

Test your fix by creating an iterator, then calling addAll on the set, then calling next() on the iterator; the CME should fire immediately. Also verify that creating a new iterator after addAll works normally, since the new iterator captures the updated modCount.

feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testAddAndRawStringNoRehash, testAddDuplicate, and testClear, first passed at run 3 when the hash index computation was corrected from division (hash/cap) to modulo (hash%cap). All four tests then regressed at run 6, where an 85-line change was made that included iterator and other functionality. The run 6 diff shows the division-to-modulo bug reappearing in one code path, indicating the code was restructured in a way that reintroduced the hash/cap bug. By run 7, a similar-sized change restored the modulo operation and all four tests passed again. The root cause in both the original failure and the regression was using integer division instead of modulo to map hash codes to bucket indices, which produces indices outside the valid array range or maps to incorrect buckets.
nextSteps: When restructuring code, keep the bucket-index computation (Math.abs(hashCode) % capacity) isolated in a single helper method so it cannot accidentally be duplicated with the wrong operator. This same per-bucket indexing pattern appears in exam problems about separate chaining, where you must identify which bucket an element lands in.
Before committing large refactors, run the full test suite to catch regressions immediately. The 4-test regression at run 6 could have been caught before adding more code on top.
Remember that hash % capacity gives a value in [0, capacity), while hash / capacity gives an unpredictable quotient. This distinction is fundamental to all hash table implementations.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent rehash failure due to hardcoded initial capacity
feedbackItems.explanation: This rehash test failed for 12 consecutive runs before passing at run 13. Early failures (runs 1-2) were ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from the division-vs-modulo bug. After that was fixed in run 3, the rehash test continued to fail with an IndexOutOfBoundsException specific to the rehash path (Index 5 out of bounds for length 5), indicating the table was not actually growing. The test likely uses a constructor with a custom initial capacity, but the initialize() method was hardcoding DEFAULT_CAPACITY for both the array allocation and the cap field. The run 13 diff shows the fix: changing `set = new Node[DEFAULT_CAPACITY]` to `set = new Node[initialCapacity]` and `cap = DEFAULT_CAPACITY` to `cap = initialCapacity`. This meant that even after checkRehash() called initialize(cap*2), the new table was still created at the default size, so elements would hash to indices beyond the array bounds. The fix ensured that the capacity parameter actually propagated through initialization.
nextSteps: When implementing rehash, the doubled capacity must flow through every step: allocate the new array at 2*oldCapacity, update the capacity field, then re-insert every element using the new capacity for index computation. Exam problems on rehashing (such as diagramming re-bucketing after a capacity doubling) test exactly this chain of updates.
Avoid hardcoding constants like DEFAULT_CAPACITY in methods that serve dual purposes (initial construction and rehash reinitialization). Use a parameterized helper so the capacity is always explicit.

Verify your load factor threshold arithmetic: with a load factor limit of 2 and initial capacity 5, rehash should trigger when size exceeds 10. Trace through the exact add count that triggers rehash and confirm the new capacity is 10.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent incorrect size return value
feedbackItems.explanation: Across all four runs, testEmptyHashSet has failed consistently. This test checks that a freshly constructed StringHashSet reports size() == 0 and isEmpty() == true. The error indicates size() is returning -1 instead of 0, which means the size field is either uninitialized or initialized to -1 in the constructor. The code changed between runs 1/3 and runs 2/4, but neither variant produced a passing test. The size field must be explicitly initialized to 0 when the hash set is constructed, and the isEmpty() method should return true when size == 0. Without correct size tracking, nearly every other test in the assignment will also fail, since add, remove, clear, and rehash all depend on an accurate element count.
nextSteps: In your constructor, ensure the size instance variable is explicitly set to 0 and that the internal bucket array is allocated (e.g., new Node[initialCapacity]). These two initializations are the foundation every other method depends on.
Implement isEmpty() to return size == 0. This is a one-line method, but it must agree with your size field, so verify that size is only modified inside add(), remove(), and clear().

After fixing the constructor, write a small main method that creates a new StringHashSet and prints size() and isEmpty() before adding anything, to confirm the baseline state is correct before moving on to add().

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent incorrect size tracking
feedbackItems.explanation: testSize has failed in all four runs with size() returning -1 both before and after add operations. This is closely related to the empty-state issue: the size field starts at -1 instead of 0, and add() does not increment it. Even if add() were partially implemented, the size would remain wrong because the field was never properly initialized. The code changed between runs 1-4 across two variants, but neither addressed size initialization or size updates inside add(). Correct size tracking requires three things: initializing size to 0 in the constructor, incrementing size by 1 each time a new (non-duplicate) element is successfully added, and decrementing size by 1 each time an element is successfully removed.
nextSteps: Initialize size to 0 in the constructor. Then, inside add(), increment size only when the element is not already present in the set (i.e., after checking for duplicates and successfully inserting a new node).
Inside remove(), decrement size only when an element is actually found and removed. Inside clear(), reset size to 0.

Test size tracking in isolation: add a few elements, print size() after each add, then remove one and print again. This will help you verify the count stays accurate before tackling more complex tests.

feedbackItems.pattern: Null output from unimplemented add/toString

Implement toRawString() to iterate over every bucket index, printing null for empty buckets and the chain of node values for non-empty ones. This gives you a visual debugging tool for verifying that add() places elements in the correct buckets.

drills.intro: Your toString is returning null elements, likely because elements aren't being stored properly in the buckets. Let's test toString with multiple elements that land in different buckets to isolate the storage issue. Paste this into StringHashSetTest.java for a point back.

Then replace the old array with the new one and update the capacity field.

feedbackItems.pattern: Recurring assertion error in SCC resolved after multiple algorithm rewrites
feedbackItems.explanation: This custom test (and the related testAMStronglyConnectedComponentExampleGraphs) failed across 11 runs, from run 34 through run 55, before finally passing. The test constructs a small directed graph and checks that stronglyConnectedComponent returns the correct set of mutually reachable vertices. At run 34, the test graph was modified (changing a C->D edge to B->D), and the SCC algorithm returned [A, B, D] instead of the expected [A, B, C, D], indicating vertex C was being missed during traversal. At run 38, a recursive subSCC helper method was introduced, replacing the iterative stack-based approach, and the test graph was adjusted to add a C->B edge. This recursive approach persisted through runs 39-50 with various modifications: run 43 fixed a null pointer by initializing checkedNodes values to empty HashSets instead of null; runs 49-50 adjusted the loop logic with labeled breaks and contingent node tracking. At run 53, the code reverted to the iterative stack-based approach, restructuring the inner loop to walk backward through the current path when a known SCC member is encountered. nextSteps: The standard SCC approach for this assignment is a two-pass reachability intersection: compute all vertices reachable forward from the key (via BFS/DFS on successors), compute all vertices reachable backward (via BFS/DFS on predecessors), and return the intersection. drills.intro: Your Milestone 2 stronglyConnectedComponent returns the SCC containing one specific key. The Final practice's graph section often asks for a related-but-different question: 'is the entire graph one big SCC?' Practice it by implementing public boolean isStronglyConnected() on your Graph<T> that returns true iff every vertex can reach every other vertex. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone2ALTest.java. As with the BFS drill, you'll need to add `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;` and `import java.util.HashSet;` at the top — neither is currently in M2ALTest's import block.
hints: Algorithm: pick any vertex v from keySet(). Do a forward BFS from v (via successorIterator) — collect every vertex it reaches. Do a reverse BFS from v (via predecessorIterator) — collect every vertex that reaches it. The graph is strongly connected iff both reachable sets equal keySet().

Why one vertex is sufficient: if v reaches everyone (forward) and everyone reaches v (reverse), then for any pair a, b, the path a → v → b exists (concatenate reverse-of-a-to-v with forward-of-v-to-b). You don't have to check V·V pairs separately.

Edge case: a single-vertex graph is trivially strongly connected — its lone vertex reaches itself with the zero-length path. Your BFS will visit only the start vertex, the reachable set is {v}, keySet() is {v}, and the comparison naturally returns true. If your code special-cases size 1 to false, you've added a bug.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented toString method returning null
feedbackItems.explanation: The toString() test has been failing since run 1 and has never passed across all 23 runs. The test expects a formatted string representation of the hash set's contents (typically a bracketed, comma-separated list like "[a, b, c]"), but the method returns null or a default value. Since working iteration logic exists for the bucket array in other methods, the toString implementation should follow a similar traversal pattern.
nextSteps: Implement toString() by iterating over every bucket in the internal array, walking each chain, and appending each element's string value to a StringBuilder. Use a separator to place commas between elements, and wrap the result in square brackets. The pattern is: start with '[', append elements separated by ', ', and close with ']'. An empty set should return '[]'.

Consider reusing your iterator (once implemented) inside toString() with a standard loop, or manually walk the bucket array. Either approach works, but the key is visiting every non-null node across all buckets.
Test edge cases: an empty set should produce '[]', and a single-element set should produce '[element]' with no trailing comma.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented iterator across all runs
feedbackItems.explanation: The iterator tests, including testIteratorDifferentReturns, testIteratorNextHasNext, testIteratorNoSuchElementException, and testIteratorConcurrentModificationException, have all been failing since run 1 with no implementation attempts across 23 runs. These four tests collectively validate the full Iterator contract for a hash set: hasNext() must correctly detect remaining elements, next() must return each element exactly once across all buckets, next() must throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted, and structural modifications to the set must trigger ConcurrentModificationException. The iterator was not implemented despite all core hash set operations being completed by run 22. This java.util.Iterator contract recurs in future assignments (EditorTrees, graphs), so building a solid understanding now is important.
nextSteps: This Iterator contract pattern recurs in every mutable collection you will build. Implement a custom inner class that implements Iterator<String>. It needs two pieces of state: (1) the current bucket index in the array, and (2) the current node within that bucket's chain. In the constructor, advance to the first non-null bucket. hasNext() returns true if the current node is non-null. next() returns the current node's value, advances to the next node in the chain, and if the chain is exhausted, scans forward to the next non-null bucket.

For fail-fast behavior, maintain a modCount field in the hash set that increments on every add, remove, or clear. When creating the iterator, snapshot modCount into an expectedModCount field. At the start of each next() call, compare the two; if they differ, throw ConcurrentModificationException. This is the standard pattern used in Java's own collections.

For the NoSuchElementException case, check hasNext() at the beginning of next(). If hasNext() is false, throw NoSuchElementException before doing anything else. This ensures the iterator signals exhaustion correctly.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented iterator traversal logic
feedbackItems.explanation: This test verifies that hasNext() and next() work correctly together to iterate over all elements in the hash set exactly once. It has failed since run 1 across all 23 runs. The core challenge for a hash set iterator is that elements are distributed across multiple buckets, and each bucket may contain a linked chain of nodes. The iterator must seamlessly traverse from one node to the next within a bucket, and then advance to the next non-empty bucket when a chain is exhausted. This is distinct from iterating a simple list or array, because many buckets may be null and must be skipped.
nextSteps: Implement hasNext() to return true whenever the current node reference is non-null. The key is ensuring that after each next() call, you eagerly advance to the next valid node: first try the current node's .next pointer, and if that is null, scan the bucket array starting from bucketIndex + 1 until you find a non-null entry or exhaust the array.

Initialize the iterator by scanning from bucket index 0 forward to find the first non-null bucket, and set the current node to that bucket's head. If no non-null bucket exists, the current node stays null and hasNext() immediately returns false.
Verify that next() returns the value before advancing the pointer. A common bug is advancing first and then returning, which skips the first element or returns the wrong one.
