feedbackItems.pattern: AM predecessor and successor iterators resolved after matrix traversal fix
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testPredecessorIterator and testSuccessorIterator for AdjacencyMatrix failed from run 2 through run 18, first passing at run 19. The code diffs show that at run 19, successorSet and predecessorSet were implemented by iterating over the matrix row/column and collecting vertices where the matrix entry equals 1, with degree methods delegating to these sets. At run 20, a similar change was applied (likely fixing a missed piece or correcting the predecessor direction). At run 27, the successor iterator's goToNext() helper was refined with comments and spacing changes, and the predecessor iterator was likely added in the same batch (48 lines added). The regressions after the initial fix show that later changes to the iterator inner classes or to shared infrastructure temporarily affected correctness before stabilizing. The test is now passing. The key correctness requirement for these iterators is scanning the correct axis of the matrix: for successors of vertex v, scan row v across all columns; for predecessors of vertex v, scan column v across all rows.
nextSteps: On the Final, graph traversal via iterators is tested under time pressure. For AdjacencyMatrix, ensure your successor iterator scans row[keyToIndex(key)] and your predecessor iterator scans column entries matrix[i][keyToIndex(key)] for all i. Mixing up row vs column is the most common directional bug.

The hasNext()/next() contract requires that next() throws NoSuchElementException when exhausted, and hasNext() is idempotent. Verify your goToNext() helper advances the index correctly and stops at matrix.length, not matrix.length-1.

When implementing iterators over a matrix, use a single columnIndex (or rowIndex) field that goToNext() advances past zero entries. Ensure goToNext() is called both in the constructor (to find the first valid entry) and after each next() call.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 7

feedbackItems.pattern: Regression in AL lazy iterator after test threshold edits
feedbackItems.explanation: This AdjacencyList predecessor lazy iteration test first passed at run 19 but regressed in later runs, failing twice before passing at run 39. The code diffs show two key change points. At run 25, the test file itself was modified: a timing assertion (endTime - startTime < 5) was commented out and the lazy threshold was relaxed from 70ms to 80ms. At run 27, the AdjacencyList iterator was substantially rewritten, replacing the SetIterator that accepted a key and string type parameter (which called successorSet/predecessorSet, eagerly building a Set) with a version that directly accepts the vertex's internal List<Vertex> of successors or predecessors. This change removed 14 lines and added 10, eliminating the eager set construction and making the iterator walk the adjacency list directly. The regression pattern shows that intermediate changes between runs 19 and 27 temporarily broke what had been working; the original iterator was backed by an eager set copy and timing-sensitive.
nextSteps: This lazy-iterator pattern recurs in the Final practice computer part, where successorIterator is called inside an inner loop; ensure your iterator's constructor does O(1) or O(degree) work by referencing the existing adjacency structure directly rather than copying into a new collection.

When writing a lazy iterator, the constructor should store only a reference to the underlying data structure and an index/cursor, not call methods like successorSet() that allocate and populate a new Set.

Test laziness independently of correctness: a correct iterator that eagerly copies data will pass neighbor_iterator tests but fail lazy_iteration tests, so verify that construction plus one next() call is O(1) relative to graph size.

feedbackItems.pattern: AM predecessor iterator row/column indexing bug fixed over many runs
feedbackItems.explanation: This AdjacencyMatrix predecessor iterator test failed from run 2 through run 16, first passing at run 17 when the bulk of AdjacencyMatrix methods (removeEdge, degree, neighbor sets, and iterators) were implemented in a 49-line addition. The test regressed and continued failing through subsequent runs. The critical fix came at run 37, where the iterator constructor was updated to properly initialize the roworcolumn flag and indexToKey map, and the hasNext/next logic was corrected to scan the matrix column (matrix[index][arrayIndex]) for predecessors rather than the row. The predecessor iterator must walk down a column of the adjacency matrix (checking matrix[i][vertexIndex] for each i) because predecessors are vertices with edges pointing to the target vertex. The 16 total failed runs reflect the difficulty of getting the row-vs-column indexing correct for both successor and predecessor iterators within a single shared iterator class. The related testSuccessorIterator had a similar trajectory, with its fix at run 38 adding the roworcolumn branching logic to distinguish row traversal (successors) from column traversal (predecessors).
nextSteps: This iterator pattern recurs in the Final practice computer part; internalize that for an adjacency matrix, successors of vertex v are found by scanning row v (matrix[v][j] for all j), while predecessors are found by scanning column v (matrix[i][v] for all i).

When a single iterator class handles both successor and predecessor traversal, ensure the constructor sets a flag that controls which dimension is iterated, and that both hasNext() and next() consistently use that flag to index the matrix correctly.
Advance the cursor past zero entries in the constructor itself so that hasNext() returns the correct value immediately after construction, not just after the first call to next().

feedbackItems.pattern: AM successor iterator row/column branching added after predecessor fix
feedbackItems.explanation: This AdjacencyMatrix successor iterator test shares the same arc as testPredecessorIterator: it first passed at run 17 with the initial bulk implementation, then regressed and failed for 17 total runs. The final fix came at run 38, one run after the predecessor iterator was corrected. The diff at run 38 shows 12 lines added that introduce an if/else branch on the roworcolumn flag: when roworcolumn is false, the iterator scans the column (matrix[index][arrayIndex]) for predecessors, and when true, it scans the row (matrix[arrayIndex][index]) for successors. hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

feedbackItems.pattern: Missing recursive contains helper, incorrect null sentinel comparison
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testContainsStrings() and testContainsInts() failed from run 20 through run 34, requiring 15 runs to resolve. The contains() method was initially stubbed to simply return false, which meant every lookup failed regardless of tree contents. The code diff at run 35 shows two key changes: first, the isEmpty() check was corrected from `root==null` to `root==NULL_NODE` (which had already been fixed in run 34 for isEmpty itself but was also present in the contains path), and second, a proper recursive helper method `contains(T item, Node n)` was introduced. This helper follows the standard BST search pattern: check for NULL_NODE as the base case (return false), then compare the item against the current node's data to decide whether to recurse left or right. Before this change, the public contains() method had no recursive traversal logic at all. The fix replaced the hardcoded `return false` with a delegation to the new recursive helper, which correctly navigates the tree structure using comparisons.
nextSteps: The BST search pattern (compare, go left or right, base case at null) recurs directly in Exam 2's shortestWordAlongPath, which navigates the tree the same way but accumulates data along the path. Practice writing this navigation pattern from scratch to build fluency.

When implementing recursive BST methods, always start by defining the base case (reaching NULL_NODE) and the recursive case (comparing the item to the current node's data to choose left or right). This three-way branching structure is the foundation of nearly every BST operation.

Be mindful of which sentinel value your tree uses. If your BST uses a NULL_NODE sentinel instead of Java null, every comparison in every method must use NULL_NODE consistently; mixing the two causes subtle bugs like the one in isEmpty() that cascaded here.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect null sentinel comparison in isEmpty()
feedbackItems.explanation: testIsEmpty() failed from run 20 through run 33, taking 14 runs to resolve. The root cause was a single-character-level bug: isEmpty() compared `root==null` instead of `root==NULL_NODE`. When a BST implementation uses a NULL_NODE sentinel object (a special static node instance representing empty subtrees), the root of an empty tree is set to NULL_NODE, not Java's null. Comparing against null would always return false, making isEmpty() report that the tree was never empty. The fix at run 34 was a one-line change, swapping `root==null` to `root==NULL_NODE`. This is a common pitfall when using the null-object pattern in tree implementations. The fact that this bug persisted for 14 runs, including a stall period from runs 30-32 with no code changes, preceded the correction.
nextSteps: The null-object pattern (NULL_NODE) is used extensively in EditorTrees, where rank computation depends on size queries that must correctly identify empty subtrees. Internalize the rule: if your tree uses a sentinel, every emptiness check in every method must compare against that sentinel, never against Java null.

When debugging a persistent failure, check all methods that test for emptiness or leaf status. A sentinel mismatch in one method (like isEmpty) can cause cascading failures in tests for other operations that depend on it.
Consider adding an assertion or comment at the top of your BST class documenting which sentinel convention you use, so you catch mismatches during code review.

feedbackItems.pattern: Broken remove algorithm across multiple cases
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testRemoveReturnValue() and testRemove() failed from run 20 through run 32, taking 13 runs to resolve before both passed at run 33. Early in this period (runs 20-23), the remove() method had compilation errors, meaning it was syntactically incomplete. By run 24, compilation was fixed but the remove logic still produced incorrect results. The stall from runs 30-32, where no code changes were made, preceded a focused fix at run 33 that corrected the remove algorithm. BST removal requires handling three distinct cases: removing a leaf node (replace with NULL_NODE), removing a node with one child (replace with that child), and removing a node with two children (find the in-order successor, swap data, then recursively remove the successor). The testRemoveReturnValue() test specifically checks that remove() returns the correct boolean indicating whether the element was found and removed, while testRemove() verifies the tree structure after removal. Both passed simultaneously at run 33, confirming the algorithm was corrected.
nextSteps: The three-case removal pattern (leaf, one child, two children with in-order successor swap) is directly reused in EditorTrees Milestone 3's delete(int pos), which adds AVL rebalancing on top. Make sure you can write all three cases from memory, paying special attention to the two-children case where you must find the in-order successor, copy its data, and recursively delete it from the right subtree.

When implementing remove recursively, use the pattern where each recursive call returns the (possibly updated) node reference. The parent assigns its left or right child to the return value, which naturally handles pointer updates when a node is deleted. This same pointer-replacement pattern appears in Exam 2's pruneFullSubtreesSize3.
Test remove() incrementally: first verify leaf removal works, then single-child removal, then two-child removal. Isolating cases helps identify which branch of the logic is broken.

feedbackItems.pattern: AM iterator and lazy iteration stubs resolved in runs 24-26
feedbackItems.explanation: The tests testSuccessorIterator, testSuccessorIteratorIsLazy, testPredecessorIterator, and testPredecessorIteratorIsLazy all failed from run 12 through the mid-20s because the AdjacencyMatrixGraph iterator methods were left as stubs returning null. The initial AM class was introduced at run 12 with only constructor and hasVertex working; runs 13-14 dealt with visibility issues around the inner Vertex class; runs 15-16 established basic edge operations. The iterator methods were not implemented until run 24, when 37 lines were added to AdjacencyMatrixGraph replacing the TODO stubs for successorIterator and successorSet (and likely predecessorIterator/predecessorSet). The code diff shows the neighbor-set logic scanning the matrix row for 1-entries and collecting keys into a HashSet. The successor iterator and its laziness test both passed at run 24. The predecessor iterator required an additional change at run 26 (57 lines added), completing the column-scanning logic for predecessors. Notably, the laziness tests also passed, which means the iterator implementations walk the matrix indices on demand rather than pre-building a full Set. The long failure window (12 runs for successor, 14 for predecessor) reflects the incremental build order; core operations were established first, then neighbor sets, then iterators.
nextSteps: This lazy-iterator pattern recurs in the Final practice computer part, where successorIterator is called inside an inner loop; if the iterator eagerly builds a Set on construction, the performance test will time out. Practice writing iterators that maintain a cursor index and advance it in next(), scanning the matrix row or column only as far as needed.

For matrix-based graphs, a lazy predecessor iterator should walk column entries (matrix[j][row]) and a lazy successor iterator should walk row entries (matrix[row][j]). Make sure you understand why the scan direction differs and how the index-to-key mapping translates matrix positions back to vertex keys.

Verify that your iterators throw NoSuchElementException when next() is called past the end, per the java.util.Iterator contract. This is a common oversight when the cursor-advancement logic silently returns null instead of throwing.

drills.intro: The Final's graph programming section asks you to extend Graph<T> with a new traversal method on top of your Milestone 1 work. Practice that exact pattern by adding a public int numDirectedTriangles() method to your Graph<T> (or its AL/AM subclasses) that returns the number of directed 3-cycles in the graph — that is, ordered triples of distinct vertices (u, v, w) with edges u→v, v→w, w→u. Then paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java for a self-check. The simple 3-vertex case is the warm-up; harder variants follow.
hints: A directed triangle (u, v, w) requires three directed edges: u→v, v→w, and w→u. The simplest correct implementation iterates over all ordered triples of distinct vertices and checks the three edges via hasEdge — but it must not double-count.

The triple (A, B, C) and (B, C, A) and (C, A, B) describe the same triangle (a 3-cycle has three rotations). One way to count each triangle exactly once is to enforce a fixed ordering on the triple — e.g. require u to compare-less-than both v and w using vertex.toString().

If you're seeing 6 where the test expects 2, you're counting each triangle three times (once per rotation). Either divide by 3 at the end, or restrict to one canonical rotation per triangle as described above.

feedbackItems.pattern: AM predecessor laziness test resolved after successor pattern established
feedbackItems.explanation: testPredecessorIteratorIsLazy failed from run 12 through run 24, first passing at run 25. The successor-side lazy iteration tests passed one run earlier (run 24), and the predecessor side required a separate code change at run 25 adding 57 lines to AdjacencyMatrixGraph. The diff shows the same matrix-scanning pattern used for successors being adapted for predecessors: iterating over column indices (matrix[j][row]) instead of row indices (matrix[row][j]) to find incoming edges. The laziness test verifies that constructing the iterator and calling next() once completes within a tight time bound, confirming the iterator does not eagerly collect all predecessors into a Set. nextSteps: The lazy-iterator concept appears again in the Final practice computer part. To ensure laziness, your iterator constructor should only initialize a cursor position, and each call to next() should advance the cursor through the matrix column until it finds the next 1-entry, returning immediately without scanning the rest.

When implementing predecessor iteration on an adjacency matrix, remember you are scanning a column (all rows for a fixed column index), which has different cache locality characteristics than scanning a row. This matters less for correctness but is worth understanding for performance reasoning on large graphs.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

feedbackItems.pattern: AM predecessorSet stub replaced with column scan at run 23
feedbackItems.explanation: testPredecessorSet failed from run 12 through run 22, first passing at run 23. The code diff for run 23 shows 4 stub lines (TODO comments and null returns) replaced with 16 lines implementing both successorSet and predecessorSet. The visible logic scans a matrix row collecting keys where matrix[row][j] == 1 into a HashSet; the predecessorSet implementation uses the transposed scan (matrix[j][col] == 1). This test required returning a correct Set of all vertices with edges pointing to the given key. The 11-run failure window reflects the incremental development sequence: constructor and hasVertex first (run 12), then add/has edge (runs 14-15), then neighbor sets (run 23), then iterators (runs 24-26). The neighbor_sets category is foundational because BFS shortest-path and SCC algorithms both rely on successorSet/predecessorSet to discover reachable vertices.
nextSteps: BFS and DFS trace tables on the Final practice paper section list the successor set of each visited vertex at every step. Make sure you can mentally trace how successorSet and predecessorSet map to row-scanning and column-scanning in the adjacency matrix, respectively.

The returned Set should be a snapshot (defensive copy), not a live view of internal state. If a caller modifies the returned Set, it must not corrupt the graph's adjacency matrix. Confirm your implementation creates a new HashSet rather than exposing an internal collection.

For predecessorSet on an adjacency matrix, the key insight is that predecessors of vertex v correspond to all rows i where matrix[i][indexOf(v)] == 1. This column scan is O(V) regardless of the actual in-degree, which contrasts with the adjacency list representation where predecessorSet can be O(in-degree).

feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testRemove() and testRemoveAdvanced(), has been failing since run 3 across all 50 attempts. After compilation issues were resolved at run 12, the errors shifted from undefined-method failures to assertion failures, indicating that remove() executes but produces incorrect results. The test specifically checks that remove() returns the correct boolean: true when an element was found and removed, false when it was not present. Runs 47-52 show no change in results. The testRemoveIllegalArgumentException passes since run 12, confirming that the method signature and exception-throwing logic are correct. The core removal logic and its return value do not match expected behavior. The three removal cases (leaf, one-child, two-children) recur in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) applies these patterns with AVL rebalancing on top.
nextSteps: The three-case BST removal pattern (leaf, one child, two children via in-order successor) recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3 with AVL rebalancing layered on top. Master it now by writing out, on paper, what happens to the tree structure for each case: leaf nodes get replaced by NULL_NODE, one-child nodes get replaced by their single child, and two-children nodes swap data with their in-order successor before removing that successor.

Ensure your recursive remove helper returns the updated subtree root (the node that should replace the current node in the parent's left or right pointer), and that the caller assigns this return value back: e.g., node.left = removeHelper(node.left, element). Use a separate boolean field or wrapper to track whether the element was actually found, and return that boolean from the public remove() method.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent assertion failure in remove correctness
feedbackItems.explanation: testRemove() has failed since run 3 across all runs through run 52, sharing the same root cause as testRemoveReturnValue() and testRemoveAdvanced(). All three remove tests transitioned from compilation errors to assertion failures at run 12, confirming the method exists and runs but does not correctly update the tree structure after removal. The test likely checks that after removing elements, contains() returns false for removed elements and the tree's size and structure are correct. Across 50 attempts, no distinct changes in failure pattern have occurred. The underlying issue is most likely in how the recursive helper reassigns child pointers after a removal, or in how the two-children case (finding and removing the in-order successor) is handled.
nextSteps: Focus on the pointer-replacement pattern: every recursive call in your remove helper should return the (possibly updated) root of that subtree, and the parent must capture it with node.left = remove(node.left, elem) or node.right = remove(node.right, elem). If you skip this reassignment, the tree structure never actually changes even though you found the node to remove.

For the two-children case, find the in-order successor (the leftmost node in the right subtree), copy its data into the current node, then recursively remove the successor from the right subtree. Make sure you are removing the successor's value, not the original value, from the right subtree.

Add print statements or use a debugger to print the tree's toString() output before and after each remove call on a small example. Compare the actual output to what you expect. This will quickly reveal whether nodes are being detached or just ignored.

feedbackItems.pattern: NullPointerException in pre-order iterator initialization
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed at run 8 with a NullPointerException, which was the only run where it produced a result. The failure occurred when attempting to implement preOrderIterator() with a stack-based approach; the stack initialization contained a null pointer error. Pre-order traversal visits the current node first, then pushes the right child and left child onto the stack in that order, so the left child is processed first. A common source of NullPointerException is pushing null children onto the stack or failing to check for NULL_NODE before accessing node fields. This traversal concept recurs directly in EditorTrees toString(), HW6 preOrderInOrderBuild, and Exam 3.
nextSteps: Pre-order iterator understanding is tested in HW6 (preOrderInOrderBuild) and Exam 3. The correct stack-based algorithm is: initialize by pushing the root onto the stack. In hasNext(), return whether the stack is non-empty. In next(), pop the top node, push its right child (if not NULL_NODE), then push its left child (if not NULL_NODE), and return the popped node's data. Always guard against pushing NULL_NODE onto the stack.

Check that your iterator constructor handles the case where the tree is empty (root is NULL_NODE). In that case, the stack should remain empty and hasNext() should immediately return false. If you push NULL_NODE onto the stack, subsequent calls to next() will dereference null fields.

Verify that your hasNext() method checks stack.isEmpty() rather than checking a node reference for null. If hasNext() is based on a current-node field that was never initialized, it will either always return true (infinite loop) or throw a NullPointerException.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent assertion failure in in-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: testIterator() has failed from run 3 through run 52 across all attempts. After compilation issues were resolved at run 12, the failure shifted to assertion errors, meaning the iterator runs but produces incorrect traversal output or incorrect hasNext() behavior. The stack-based in-order iterator must push all left descendants of the root initially, then on each next() call, pop the top node, return its value, and push all left descendants of its right child. If hasNext() checks the wrong condition (for example, a node field instead of stack emptiness), it will report incorrect availability of elements. This same in-order traversal pattern is used in EditorTrees toString() and is tested on Exam 3.
nextSteps: In-order traversal via iterator is foundational for EditorTrees toString() and Exam 3. The correct stack-based algorithm: in the constructor, push the root and then repeatedly push each node's left child until you reach NULL_NODE. In next(), pop the top node, save its data, then push the popped node's right child and all of that child's left descendants. hasNext() simply returns !stack.isEmpty().

A common bug is initializing hasNext() based on whether a 'current' node reference is null rather than checking the stack. If you use a current-node field, make sure it is updated correctly after every next() call, or better yet, rely solely on the stack's emptiness as the termination condition.

Trace your iterator by hand on a small tree (e.g., insert 4, 2, 6, 1, 3). The in-order output should be [1, 2, 3, 4, 6]. Write down the stack contents after each next() call and verify they match what you expect.

feedbackItems.pattern: Late AdjacencyMatrix implementation required many runs to begin
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testHasVertex, testSuccessorIteratorIsLazy, testHasEdge, testInDegree, testNumEdges, testPredecessorSet, testAddEdge, testSuccessorIterator, testRemoveEdge, testOutDegree, testSuccessorSet, and testConstructorAndSize for AdjacencyMatrix, all failed from Run 1 through Run 63 because the AdjacencyMatrix class was entirely unimplemented. The first passing run was Run 64, when the constructor was written to populate keyToIndex (a Map from key to integer index) and indexToKey (a List for reverse lookup), and methods like hasVertex, hasEdge, and addEdge were implemented against the matrix representation. Run 66 cleaned up an unused import of AdjacencyListGraph.Vertex. Run 74-75 then added predecessorSet, successorSet, and iterator implementations for AM, completing the remaining AM tests. The 30 failed runs reflect the sequencing of implementing AL first and AM second; the gap between completing AL (around Run 36) and starting AM (Run 64) spanned roughly 28 runs.
nextSteps: On the Final's coding section, you will need to implement a method in both AL and AM forms; practice translating between the two representations so you can implement AM without needing to finish AL first as a reference.

It first passed at Run 105, when the algorithm was written as two helper methods: searchForward (collecting all vertices reachable from key via successors) and searchBackwards (collecting all vertices that can reach key via predecessors), with the SCC being their intersection. Both helpers initially used recursion. This worked for small example graphs but caused a StackOverflowError on the large Wikipedia graph (460k vertices). Runs 114 and 115 show the conversion of searchBackwards from a recursive approach (with base case checking visitedSet.contains and iterating over predecessorSet) to an iterative approach using an explicit ArrayDeque as a stack. Recursive DFS hits Java's default stack limit around 10k-20k frames, which is far below the 460k vertices in the Wikipedia graph. Make iterative traversal your standard pattern.

When computing SCC as the intersection of forward-reachable and backward-reachable sets, verify correctness by checking that the starting vertex is always in both sets and therefore always in the result. Testing on small hand-drawn graphs with known SCCs (e.g., a cycle of 3 vs. a chain of 3) builds intuition for the algorithm.

drills.intro: Your Milestone 2 stronglyConnectedComponent returns the SCC containing one specific key. The Final practice's graph section often asks for a related-but-different question: 'is the entire graph one big SCC?' Practice it by implementing public boolean isStronglyConnected() on your Graph<T> that returns true iff every vertex can reach every other vertex. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone2ALTest.java. As with the BFS drill, you'll need to add `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;` and `import java.util.HashSet;` at the top — neither is currently in M2ALTest's import block.
hints: Algorithm: pick any vertex v from keySet(). Do a forward BFS from v (via successorIterator) — collect every vertex it reaches. Do a reverse BFS from v (via predecessorIterator) — collect every vertex that reaches it. The graph is strongly connected iff both reachable sets equal keySet().

Why one vertex is sufficient: if v reaches everyone (forward) and everyone reaches v (reverse), then for any pair a, b, the path a → v → b exists (concatenate reverse-of-a-to-v with forward-of-v-to-b). You don't have to check V·V pairs separately.

Edge case: a single-vertex graph is trivially strongly connected — its lone vertex reaches itself with the zero-length path. Your BFS will visit only the start vertex, the reachable set is {v}, keySet() is {v}, and the comparison naturally returns true. If your code special-cases size 1 to false, you've added a bug.

Named inner classes (like SuccIterator) are preferable to anonymous classes when the iterator needs to capture mutable state (like an index), because the scoping rules are clearer and debugging is easier. This pattern applies to any Iterator you write in future assignments.

The triple (A, B, C) and (B, C, A) and (C, A, B) describe the same triangle (a 3-cycle has three rotations). One way to count each triangle exactly once is to enforce a fixed ordering on the triple — e.g. require u to compare-less-than both v and w using vertex.toString().

feedbackItems.pattern: AM predecessor iterator implemented late after AL completion
feedbackItems.explanation: This test verifies that predecessorIterator returns a correct Iterator<T> over a vertex's predecessors in the AdjacencyMatrix representation. It failed for 40 runs (Runs 1-75) and first passed at Run 76. The extended failure period reflects two phases: first, the AdjacencyMatrix class was entirely unimplemented until Run 64, and second, the predecessor iterator specifically was not added until Run 74-76. For AM, a predecessor iterator must scan column j of the adjacency matrix (where j is the index of the target vertex) and yield indexToKey(i) for each row i where matrix[i][j] == 1. This is inherently different from the AL predecessor iterator, which walks a predecessors list. No code diffs are provided specifically for Run 76, but the Run 74-75 diffs show predecessorSet and related methods being added to AdjacencyMatrixGraph, and the iterator followed the same column-scanning pattern. The test required multiple attempts across Runs 74-76 to stabilize.
nextSteps: The Final's graph coding section may require iterating over predecessors or successors in AM form; remember that for AM, successors of vertex i are found by scanning row i (matrix[i][*]), while predecessors of vertex j are found by scanning column j (matrix[*][j]). Getting this row-vs-column distinction wrong is the most common AM iterator bug.

For a lazy AM predecessor iterator, store the target column index and a current-row cursor. In hasNext(), scan forward from the cursor to find the next row with a 1 in that column, without building a Set. In next(), return indexToKey of that row and advance the cursor. This ensures O(1) construction time.
Test your AM iterators on a graph where a vertex has no predecessors (empty iteration), exactly one predecessor, and multiple predecessors to verify boundary conditions in the column scan.

courseAppearances.label: java.util.Iterator contract

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

feedbackItems.pattern: Regression from refactoring challenge-pair code broke shortestPath test
feedbackItems.explanation: This test first passed at run 37, confirming that the BFS-based shortestPath works correctly on the 460k-vertex Wikipedia living-people graph. Starting at run 39, the test began failing and has not recovered through run 42. The diffs show that at run 39, the stub stronglyConnectedComponent methods were removed from both AdjacencyListGraph and AdjacencyMatrixGraph, the SCC logic was moved into Graph (replacing the naive double-shortestPath approach with a forward/reverse reachability intersection), and a findLongestShortestPath method was added with multithreaded search logic, file I/O (PrintWriter, FileWriter), and synchronized collections. Runs 41 and 42 show continued iteration on this challenge-pair search code, adding logging infrastructure and adjusting seed pool sizes. The semantic context confirms that each of these runs failed due to code that could not compile: undefined methods, type mismatches, and syntax errors, all located in the new findLongestShortestPath code rather than in shortestPath itself. Because the test file and the new method share the same compilation unit (graphs.Graph), any syntax or type error in the challenge-pair code prevents the entire class from compiling, which causes the shortestPath test to abort even though the shortestPath logic itself is unchanged and correct.
nextSteps: This performance discipline pattern recurs in the Final practice computer part, where graph traversals must finish within a time bound; isolate experimental code (like the challenge-pair search) into a separate method or class so that incomplete edits do not block compilation of working methods like shortestPath.

When adding complex features like multithreaded BFS with file I/O, compile and test after each small addition rather than writing 70+ lines at once; this prevents cascading type errors from hiding in a large diff.

Review the current state of graphs.Graph for any unclosed braces, unresolved imports (FileWriter, PrintWriter), or references to methods that were renamed or removed (e.g., bfsFarthestWithDist); fixing these will restore the passing shortestPath test without any algorithmic changes.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incremental addEdge fixes across exception handling and duplicate detection
feedbackItems.explanation: The testAddEdge test failed from runs 1 through 4 before first passing at run 5, then briefly regressed at run 6 before stabilizing. The initial failures (runs 1-3) showed the method returning false. At run 4, the error shifted from "expected true but was false" to "Did not throw NoSuchElementException," indicating edge-insertion logic was added but the exception for missing endpoints was not yet implemented. The run 5 diff shows the NoSuchElementException declaration was added and addEdge was implemented with proper vertex lookup, which fixed the test. At run 6, the error changed to "expected false but was true," meaning the duplicate-edge check was broken: addEdge was returning true even when the edge already existed. The same diff structure appears at runs 5, 6, and 7 (the diff tool shows the cumulative change from the original stub), and by run 7 the test passed and remained passing through run 18. The method required three distinct behaviors: throwing for missing vertices, returning true for a new edge, and returning false for a duplicate.
nextSteps: Every graph drill on the Final starts by building a graph via addEdge calls, so internalize the three-part contract: (1) throw NoSuchElementException if either endpoint is absent, (2) return false if the edge already exists, (3) add the edge and return true otherwise. Writing these as explicit guard clauses in order prevents the kind of regression seen at run 6.

When addEdge modifies both the successor list of 'from' and the predecessor list of 'to', verify that the duplicate check inspects the correct collection before insertion; checking successors of 'from' is sufficient for a directed graph.
Use a small test case with two vertices and one edge to manually trace through your addEdge logic for both the first-add (true) and duplicate-add (false) cases before running the full test suite.

hints: A directed triangle (u, v, w) requires three directed edges: u→v, v→w, and w→u. The simplest correct implementation iterates over all ordered triples of distinct vertices and checks the three edges via hasEdge — but it must not double-count.

The triple (A, B, C) and (B, C, A) and (C, A, B) describe the same triangle (a 3-cycle has three rotations). One way to count each triangle exactly once is to enforce a fixed ordering on the triple — e.g. require u to compare-less-than both v and w using vertex.toString().

If you're seeing 6 where the test expects 2, you're counting each triangle three times (once per rotation). Either divide by 3 at the end, or restrict to one canonical rotation per triangle as described above.

feedbackItems.pattern: Lazy successor iterator resolved after 14 runs of eager implementation
feedbackItems.explanation: The testSuccessorIteratorIsLazy test failed for 14 consecutive runs (runs 1-14) before passing at run 15. For the first several runs, the iterator methods were not implemented at all. Once basic graph operations (addEdge, hasEdge, neighbor sets) were working, the initial iterator implementation returned successorSet(key).iterator(), which delegates to an eagerly constructed Set. The lazy iteration test measures the time to construct the iterator and call next() once; if this time is proportional to the degree of the vertex rather than the size of the entire neighbor set, it passes. At run 15, the diff shows the one-liner was replaced with a custom anonymous Iterator<T> that wraps the internal v1.successors.iterator(), adding a NoSuchElementException check for missing keys. This approach is lazy because it does not copy the successor collection into a new Set; it traverses the underlying data structure on demand. The predecessorIterator was fixed similarly at run 11 (in a batch that also implemented many other methods), but the successor version required the additional run 15 fix.
nextSteps: This lazy iteration pattern recurs in the Final practice computer part, where successorIterator is called inside an inner loop and an eager implementation will time out; always wrap the internal collection's own iterator rather than building a new Set.

Understand the distinction between lazy and eager: a lazy iterator defers work to each hasNext()/next() call, while an eager one does all work upfront in the constructor. If your iterator's constructor calls successorSet() or allocates a HashSet, it is eager regardless of what next() does.

Practice writing anonymous Iterator<T> implementations that delegate to an underlying iterator, translating Vertex objects to keys of type T in the next() method; this pattern applies to any graph representation.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

nextSteps: The Final's graph traversal questions rely on correct iterator behavior; when writing a custom Iterator<T> that wraps an internal Iterator<Vertex>, make sure next() performs the Vertex-to-key translation and that hasNext() delegates directly without side effects.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method as the warm-up, now on a 6-vertex example from the Final practice's computer part. The graph below has exactly 3 directed triangles after all 9 edges are added. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the simple case passes. If your count is wildly off, the bug is usually rotation-double-counting; if it's off by one or two, you may be misreading the edge list — sketch the adjacency list on paper first.
hints: Build the adjacency list on paper before running. From A: A→B. From B: B→C, B→D. From C: C→A, C→E, C→F. From D: D→E. From E: E→B, E→F. From F: nothing. With those edges in hand, scan for closed 3-cycles by inspection — that gives you the answer to compare against your code.

If you're seeing 9 instead of 3, you're counting each of the three triangles three times (one per rotation). If you're seeing 6 or 18, you're counting both rotations AND reflections — but in a directed graph there is no reflection symmetry, so check your loop bounds.

A reliable iteration shape: for u in keySet(), for v in successorSet(u), for w in successorSet(v) — if hasEdge(w, u) and {u,v,w} are pairwise distinct, increment. Then divide the running count by 3 once at the end.

Early runs (3-4) had compilation issues that prevented execution entirely. From run 5 onward, other methods (insert, toArray, toArrayList, iterators) were added while remove() remained unimplemented. The remove() method handles three distinct cases: removing a leaf node (replace with NULL_NODE), removing a node with one child (replace with that child), and removing a node with two children (find the in-order successor, copy its data, then recursively remove the successor). The recursive helper returns the updated subtree root so that the parent's child pointer is correctly reassigned. All four tests, including the edge case for IllegalArgumentException on null input, passed on the first implementation attempt in run 16.

Understand why the recursive remove helper must return the (possibly updated) node reference: when a node is deleted, its parent needs to update its left or right pointer. This pointer-replacement pattern, where returning NULL_NODE detaches a subtree, appears again in Exam 2's pruneFullSubtreesSize3 problem.

For the IllegalArgumentException edge case, ensure that null-checking happens at the public method level before any recursive traversal begins. This separation of validation from recursion is a clean pattern to apply consistently across tree operations.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented method, resolved after incremental build-up
feedbackItems.explanation: The in-order iterator test failed from run 3 through run 14, then passed at run 15 when a 31-line addition introduced the InOrderIterator inner class. Early runs (3-4) failed due to compilation issues, and runs 5-14 focused on implementing other methods (insert, toArray, toArrayList, inefficientIterator, preOrderIterator). The iterator implementation uses a stack-based approach: the constructor pushes all left-spine nodes onto the stack, and each call to next() pops the top node, returns its value, then pushes the left spine of that node's right child. This is the standard O(h) space, O(n) total time in-order traversal without recursion. The implementation passed on the first attempt in run 15.
nextSteps: The stack-based in-order traversal pattern directly parallels EditorTrees toString(), which must run in O(N) via in-order traversal. Solidify your understanding of why pushing the left spine simulates the recursive call stack: each stack frame represents a node whose left subtree has been fully visited but whose own value and right subtree remain.

Practice converting between recursive and iterative tree traversals for all three orders (in-order, pre-order, post-order). Exam 3 and the Final list traversals and iterators as explicit topics, and understanding the stack-based approach for each order will help you predict traversal outputs and implement them efficiently.

Verify that your iterator correctly handles hasNext() by checking whether the stack is empty, and that it throws NoSuchElementException when next() is called on an exhausted iterator. These edge cases are easy to overlook but important for correctness.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method as the warm-up, now on a 6-vertex example from the Final practice's computer part. The graph below has exactly 3 directed triangles after all 9 edges are added. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java after the simple case passes. If your count is wildly off, the bug is usually rotation-double-counting; if it's off by one or two, you may be misreading the edge list — sketch the adjacency list on paper first.
hints: Build the adjacency list on paper before running. From A: A→B. From B: B→C, B→D. From C: C→A, C→E, C→F. From D: D→E. From E: E→B, E→F. From F: nothing. With those edges in hand, scan for closed 3-cycles by inspection — that gives you the answer to compare against your code.

If you're seeing 9 instead of 3, you're counting each of the three triangles three times (one per rotation). If you're seeing 6 or 18, you're counting both rotations AND reflections — but in a directed graph there is no reflection symmetry, so check your loop bounds.

A reliable iteration shape: for u in keySet(), for v in successorSet(u), for w in successorSet(v) — if hasEdge(w, u) and {u,v,w} are pairwise distinct, increment. Then divide the running count by 3 once at the end.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

feedbackItems.pattern: SCC on large Wikipedia graph required iterative rewrite over 65 attempts
feedbackItems.explanation: This wiki_surfing SCC test failed from run 105 through run 169, requiring 65 attempts to resolve. The progression shows three distinct phases: initial assertion failures (runs 105-122) where the SCC algorithm returned incorrect results on the 460k-vertex Wikipedia graph; a StackOverflowError phase (runs 123 onward) indicating recursive DFS exceeded the call stack on the large graph; and a partial-results phase (runs 124-169) where the StackOverflowError was resolved but the algorithm returned incomplete strongly connected components (for example, finding only 3 of 6 members). The breakthrough at run 170 shows a significant refactoring: the predecessorConnected collection was changed from a Set to a List with a separate visited Set (ps), and the traversal was converted to an iterative approach using index tracking (while loop with size comparison). This pattern of maintaining a worklist with an index variable and checking predecessorConnected.size() != index is a standard iterative BFS/DFS replacement for recursion. The test passed from run 170 onward through run 179.
nextSteps: This performance discipline recurs on the Final, where graph traversal is graded for O(N+E) on a moderately-sized graph. For SCC computation, both forward reachability (successors) and reverse reachability (predecessors) must be computed iteratively using an explicit stack or queue rather than recursion, since real-world graphs can have components with thousands of vertices that exceed the default call stack.

The SCC algorithm computes the intersection of forward-reachable and backward-reachable vertex sets from a given vertex. Ensure both traversals use a visited set to avoid revisiting vertices, and that the worklist (stack or queue) processes every reachable vertex before computing the intersection. A partial result typically means the traversal terminated early due to a missing visited check or premature loop exit.

When converting recursive DFS to iterative, use an explicit Stack<T> (for DFS) or Queue<T> (for BFS). Push/enqueue unvisited neighbors, mark them visited immediately upon discovery (not upon processing), and continue until the worklist is empty. This guarantees complete reachability.

feedbackItems.explanation: The testPredecessorIteratorIsLazy test failed from run 1 through run 53, passing first at run 54 in the same code change that fixed testPredecessorIterator. This test verifies that constructing the iterator and calling next() once completes within a tight time bound, confirming the iterator does not eagerly build a Set of all predecessors on construction. For the AdjacencyMatrix representation, laziness is naturally achieved because the iterator simply scans the column of the boolean/int matrix one entry at a time; there is no collection to pre-build. Both the correctness test and the laziness test passed simultaneously at run 54, indicating the implementation was correctly structured as a column-scanning iterator rather than an eager Set-based approach. The diff shows the PredecessorIterator inner class was created with direct matrix access, which inherently satisfies the laziness requirement.
nextSteps: On the Final, the graph problem includes a performance-bound test after the correctness test for iterators. For AdjacencyMatrix, laziness means the constructor does O(1) or O(first-neighbor) work, not O(V) work. The iterator advances through the column on each next() call. Understand why this is naturally lazy for a matrix but requires more care for an adjacency list.

For AdjacencyList, laziness means wrapping the underlying collection's iterator rather than copying into a new Set. For AdjacencyMatrix, laziness means scanning the row or column incrementally. Both representations should have O(1) iterator construction cost, with the per-element cost being O(1) for lists and O(gap) for matrices where gap is the distance to the next nonzero entry.

feedbackItems.pattern: Relative speed tests failing since first appearance, never revisited
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testRelativeSpeedforRemoveEdge and testRelativeSpeedforOutDegree first appeared in run 6 and were last attempted in run 18, failing both times. These relative_speed tests compare the wall-clock performance of AdjacencyList vs AdjacencyMatrix for specific operations, verifying that each representation exhibits the expected big-O behavior. For removeEdge, AdjacencyMatrix should be O(1) (set a cell to 0) while AdjacencyList is O(degree) (scan a list). For outDegree, AdjacencyList should be O(1) (return list size) while AdjacencyMatrix is O(V) (scan a row). If either representation uses the wrong internal data structure or performs unnecessary work, the speed ratio will not match expectations and the test fails. With only 2 failed runs and no code diffs captured for these tests, the speed tests were enabled briefly but not revisited. Later runs (up through run 98) focused on correctness and Milestone 2 algorithms, leaving these speed tests unaddressed.
nextSteps: This AL-vs-AM performance reasoning recurs on the Final's paper section, where you must pick a representation for a given workload and justify in big-O terms. For removeEdge: AdjacencyMatrix should flip a single matrix cell in O(1), while AdjacencyList must locate and remove from a list in O(degree). Verify your AM removeEdge does not iterate over neighbors or rebuild data structures.

For outDegree: AdjacencyList should return the successor list's size in O(1), not iterate. AdjacencyMatrix must scan an entire row in O(V). If your AL outDegree iterates or your AM outDegree caches the count, the relative speed ratio will be inverted. Check that each method's complexity matches the representation's theoretical guarantee.

Run the speed tests in isolation with speedTestsOn = true and compare the measured times. If the ratio is close to the threshold, consider whether your graph construction or edge-count bookkeeping is adding hidden overhead to one representation.

feedbackItems.pattern: numEdges unimplemented for 40 runs, fixed by summing successor list sizes
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed from run 1 through run 40, a span of 40 runs where numEdges() was not returning the correct total edge count for the AdjacencyList representation. The semantic context shows the initial implementation had the constructor and size() working but edge operations were not yet implemented, and no code changes were detected across runs 1-5 and likely many subsequent runs. The fix in run 41 introduced a loop over all vertices in keyToVertex, summing each vertex's successors.size() to compute the total edge count. The same diff also added NoSuchElementException guards to the iterator methods and refactored the successor and predecessor iterators to use post-increment indexing (curr[0]++). The numEdges approach of summing successor list sizes is correct for a directed graph since each directed edge appears exactly once in some vertex's successor list. The test has passed stably from run 41 onward through run 82.
nextSteps: On the Final's coding section, you will build graphs via addEdge calls and may need to report edge counts. Understand the two common strategies: (1) maintain a running counter incremented/decremented in addEdge/removeEdge, or (2) compute on the fly by summing adjacency sizes. The counter approach gives O(1) numEdges but requires careful bookkeeping in both addEdge and removeEdge; the summation approach is O(V) but simpler to keep correct.

Verify that your removeEdge method keeps numEdges consistent. If you use a running counter, decrement it only when an edge actually existed. If you compute on the fly, removeEdge just needs to update the adjacency structure and numEdges will reflect the change automatically.

Review the interaction between numEdges and addEdge's boolean return: addEdge should return false (and not increment any counter) when the edge already exists. A mismatch here causes numEdges to over-count.

feedbackItems.pattern: AL predecessor iterator non-lazy due to eager index and off-by-one logic
feedbackItems.explanation: This lazy_iteration test for the AdjacencyList predecessor iterator failed from run 1 through run 38. The test checks that constructing the iterator and calling next() once completes within a tight time bound, which fails if the iterator eagerly copies the predecessor list into a new collection at construction time. The code diff at run 39 shows the fix: the predecessor iterator's hasNext() was changed from checking curr[0] + 1 < size (an off-by-one that would also skip the last element) to curr[0] < size, and next() was simplified to return predecessors.get(curr[0]++).key using post-increment. The successor iterator received the same refactoring. Additionally, NoSuchElementException guards were added for missing keys. These changes ensured the iterator walks the existing list lazily, indexing into it on each next() call rather than copying. The test has passed from run 39 onward.
nextSteps: The Final's graph coding problem traverses via successorIterator in an inner loop; a non-lazy iterator that copies neighbors on construction will time out. The lazy pattern is: store only an index (or a reference to the underlying collection plus a cursor), advance the cursor in next(), and check bounds in hasNext(). No new collection should be allocated in the iterator constructor.

When writing hasNext()/next() pairs, be precise about pre-increment vs post-increment and the boundary check. hasNext() should return curr < size (not curr + 1 < size), and next() should return the element at curr and then increment. An off-by-one in hasNext causes either a skipped last element or an IndexOutOfBoundsException.
Test your iterators with a single-element list to catch boundary bugs: hasNext() should return true once, next() should return that element, and then hasNext() should return false.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

feedbackItems.pattern: AM predecessor iterator required row/column rewrite for lazy matrix scanning
feedbackItems.explanation: This lazy_iteration test for the AdjacencyMatrix predecessor iterator failed across 36 runs (runs 43-78). The semantic context shows a progression of distinct error types: the initial AM implementation threw null returns (run 43-45), then NoSuchElementException (run 46), then NullPointerException from Map.get() returning null (run 47), indicating multiple approaches were attempted for mapping keys to matrix indices. The fix at run 79 was a substantial rewrite (12 lines removed, 20 added) that correctly captured the row index from keyToIndex.get(key) at iterator construction time, then implemented hasNext() by scanning forward through the matrix column/row with a while loop that skips zero entries (while next[0] < matrix.length && matrix[row][next[0]] == 0). This is the correct lazy pattern for a matrix-backed graph: no collection is built up front; instead, the iterator scans the matrix on demand. The predecessor iterator specifically needs to scan a column (fixed row index varies over columns), while the successor iterator scans a row. The test has passed from run 79 onward through run 83.
nextSteps: For the Final's graph coding problem, you may need to write iterators over matrix representations. The key distinction: a successor iterator for vertex v scans row v (matrix[v][col] for increasing col), while a predecessor iterator scans column v (matrix[row][v] for increasing row). Mixing up row vs column is the most common bug. Verify your implementation uses the correct fixed dimension for each.

The lazy scanning pattern for a matrix iterator is: in hasNext(), advance the cursor past all zero entries until you find a 1 or exhaust the dimension. In next(), return the key at the current cursor position and advance past it. This avoids allocating a neighbor set and ensures O(1) construction time, which is what the laziness test measures.

Consider edge cases: a vertex with no predecessors (the entire column is zeros) should yield an iterator where hasNext() returns false immediately. Test this scenario to confirm your while-loop termination condition is correct.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method as the warm-up, now on a 6-vertex example from the Final practice's computer part. The graph below has exactly 3 directed triangles after all 9 edges are added. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1AMTest.java after the simple case passes. If your count is wildly off, the bug is usually rotation-double-counting; if it's off by one or two, you may be misreading the edge list — sketch the adjacency list on paper first.
hints: Build the adjacency list on paper before running. From A: A→B. From B: B→C, B→D. From C: C→A, C→E, C→F. From D: D→E. From E: E→B, E→F. From F: nothing. With those edges in hand, scan for closed 3-cycles by inspection — that gives you the answer to compare against your code.

If you're seeing 9 instead of 3, you're counting each of the three triangles three times (one per rotation). If you're seeing 6 or 18, you're counting both rotations AND reflections — but in a directed graph there is no reflection symmetry, so check your loop bounds.

A reliable iteration shape: for u in keySet(), for v in successorSet(u), for w in successorSet(v) — if hasEdge(w, u) and {u,v,w} are pairwise distinct, increment. Then divide the running count by 3 once at the end.

feedbackItems.explanation: All four iterator-related tests, including testIteratorDifferentReturns(), testIteratorNextHasNext(), testIteratorNoSuchElementException(), and testIteratorConcurrentModificationException(), have failed across all 33 runs because the iterator() method has not been implemented and returns null. These tests collectively verify the full java.util.Iterator contract for a hash set: hasNext() and next() must traverse all elements across all non-empty buckets, next() must throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted, and mutation of the set during iteration must trigger ConcurrentModificationException. The hasNext()/next()/NoSuchElementException contract recurs in every iterator you write for hash sets, EditorTrees, graphs, and other collections, so building a solid understanding here pays off repeatedly. Since the underlying table structure and chaining are working correctly, the iterator implementation is purely a traversal layer on top of existing, functional data.
nextSteps: Create an inner class that implements Iterator<String>. It needs two pieces of state: the current index into the table array and the current Node in the chain at that index. The constructor should advance to the first non-null bucket. hasNext() returns true if the current node is non-null. next() returns the current node's data, advances to the next node in the chain, and if the chain is exhausted, scans forward through the table array to find the next non-null bucket. Throw NoSuchElementException from next() when there are no more elements.

For ConcurrentModificationException support, maintain a modCount field in the hash set that increments on every add, remove, or clear call. The iterator's constructor captures this value as expectedModCount, and each call to hasNext() or next() checks whether modCount still matches. This fail-fast pattern recurs in every mutable collection you will build, so internalizing it now is valuable.

Verify your iterator handles sparse tables correctly: if the table has many null buckets between occupied ones, the index-scanning logic in next() must skip all of them without throwing or returning null.

This specific test validates the ConcurrentModificationException (CME) behavior: after obtaining an iterator, if the set is mutated (via add or remove), subsequent calls to the iterator's next() should detect the modification and throw CME. The modCount/expectedModCount pattern that detects mutation during iteration recurs in every mutable collection you will write. The fix is structural, requiring a modCount field on the hash set class and a snapshot of that count stored in the iterator at construction time.
nextSteps: Add an int modCount field to your hash set class and increment it in every mutating method: add(), remove(), clear(), and addAll(). In your iterator's constructor, store expectedModCount = modCount. At the start of next() (and optionally hasNext()), check if modCount != expectedModCount and throw ConcurrentModificationException if they differ.
Test this by creating an iterator, then calling add() or remove() on the set, then calling next() on the iterator. The CME should fire immediately on the next iterator operation after the mutation.
Remember that rehash is called internally by add() and should not independently increment modCount beyond what add() already does, or you may get false CME triggers.

feedbackItems.explanation: This test belongs to the same group as testIteratorDifferentReturns(), testIteratorNoSuchElementException(), and testIteratorConcurrentModificationException(). All four fail because iterator() returns null. This particular test focuses on the core hasNext()/next() contract: calling hasNext() should not advance the iterator, and calling next() should return each element exactly once. The test likely adds several elements and then iterates through them, verifying that the count of returned elements matches the set's size and that hasNext() returns false only after all elements have been consumed.
nextSteps: When implementing hasNext(), ensure it is a pure query with no side effects: it should return true if the current node reference is non-null, and false otherwise. Do not advance any pointers inside hasNext().

In next(), return the current element, then advance: first try moving to the next node in the current bucket's chain. If that chain is exhausted (node becomes null), increment the table index and scan forward until you find a non-null bucket or reach the end of the table. This two-level traversal (chain within bucket, then next bucket) is the key pattern for hash table iteration.
Consider writing a small manual test: create a set, add 3-4 elements, get an iterator, and print each call to hasNext() and next() to verify the traversal visits every element exactly once.

feedbackItems.pattern: Eager Set-backed predecessor iterator never replaced with lazy design
feedbackItems.explanation: This test (and the related AM predecessor laziness test) has been failing since run 1. In run 21, the predecessorIterator method was implemented as `return predecessorSet(key).iterator()`, which delegates to the eager predecessorSet method that materializes a full Set of predecessors before returning an iterator over it. The laziness test measures whether constructing the iterator and calling next() once completes in O(1) time rather than O(V) or O(E) time, so wrapping an eager Set in .iterator() will always fail this check. Runs 46 and 47 included renaming and refactoring of SCC helper methods but did not modify the iterator implementation. The predecessorIterator method continues to call predecessorSet, which builds a complete Set before any iteration begins. The AM version has the same problem, with predecessorIterator similarly backed by predecessorSet.
nextSteps: This lazy-iterator pattern recurs in the Final practice computer part, where successorIterator is called inside an inner loop and an eager implementation will time out. Write a custom Iterator<T> class (anonymous or named) whose constructor does minimal work: for AdjacencyListGraph, store a reference to the predecessor list and obtain its internal iterator; for AdjacencyMatrixGraph, store the current scan index in the boolean matrix row/column. hasNext() and next() should advance one neighbor at a time without ever building a Set.

For AdjacencyMatrixGraph specifically, the predecessor iterator should scan the adjacency column for the given vertex. Store the column index and a row cursor as fields. In hasNext(), advance the cursor until you find a true entry or exhaust the rows. This yields O(1) amortized per call without allocating a collection.

After implementing lazy iterators, verify that your predecessorSet and successorSet methods are NOT called by the iterator methods. A simple way to confirm: temporarily add a print statement in predecessorSet and check that constructing a predecessorIterator does not trigger it.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

The predecessorSet method in AdjacencyMatrixGraph scans the entire adjacency matrix column and collects all predecessors into a Set before returning, so calling .iterator() on that Set means the full scan happens at construction time. Ensure your custom iterator throws NoSuchElementException from next() when hasNext() would return false, satisfying the standard java.util.Iterator contract.

feedbackItems.pattern: Brief regression from Vertex visibility change, quickly restored
feedbackItems.explanation: This test first passed in run 2 when the AL constructor and size() method were implemented, returning keyToVertex.size(). It passed consistently through run 47. In run 48, a change made the Vertex inner class private, causing a compilation-level issue where tests referencing AdjacencyListGraph.Vertex could not access it, breaking 17 AL tests including this one. In run 49, a single-line change from `private class Vertex` to `public class Vertex` restored all 17 tests. The test is now passing again. The underlying issue is that inner class visibility in Java affects not just external callers but also test frameworks and any code that references the type across package boundaries.
nextSteps: This constructor-plus-representation pattern recurs in the Final practice computer part, where you extend Graph<T> with a fresh method. When designing inner helper classes (like Vertex), decide visibility based on whether test harnesses or subclasses need to reference the type. If the class is used only internally, package-private (default) is often sufficient, but private can block reflection-based test access.

When a single change causes many unrelated tests to fail simultaneously, treat it as a structural issue (visibility, imports, signatures) rather than a logic bug. Reverting the most recent change and re-running is the fastest diagnostic.

drills.intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.
