feedbackItems.pattern: Regression from negative hash index
feedbackItems.explanation: This test first passed at run 3 after the initial implementation of the hash set's core fields (size, Node array, version) and basic add/contains/remove logic (127 lines added). It regressed at run 6 due to an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException with index -1, which occurred because the polynomial hash function was producing negative values that were used directly as array indices. The fix at run 6 introduced a stringHashIndex helper method that attempted to handle negative hashes by adding Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1, but this approach had an overflow issue. Run 7 refined the helper to conditionally add Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 only when the hash is negative, which resolved the regression. The root cause was that Java's modulo operator (%) preserves the sign of the dividend, so a negative hash code modded by the array length yields a negative index. The test passed from run 7 onward.
nextSteps: Understand that Java's % operator is a remainder, not a true modulus: when the dividend is negative, the result is negative. The standard fix is to use Math.floorMod(hash, array.length) or to mask with & 0x7FFFFFFF before taking %. Adding Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 to a negative int can itself overflow, so prefer bitwise masking.

When writing any hash-based data structure, always centralize index computation in a single helper method (as you eventually did with stringHashIndex) so that every operation, including add, contains, remove, and rehash, uses the same safe mapping from hash code to bucket index.
Write a quick unit test with strings whose polynomial hash codes are negative to catch sign-related index bugs early, before they cascade into multiple test failures.

feedbackItems.pattern: Evolving iterator contract violations
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across 14 runs before passing at run 13. Early failures included NullPointerException in run 1 and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from negative hash indices in runs 2-5. The run 13 diff shows significant iterator restructuring: the hasNext logic was changed from a simple bounds check (overallIndex < array.length) to properly tracking the current node and advancing through chains, and the version/expectedModCount pattern for concurrent modification detection was added or corrected. The test regressed briefly around runs 18 and 20 due to changes in where version++ and size++ were placed relative to the rehash threshold check. In run 18, the ordering of version increment and size increment was adjusted, and in run 20, the rehash condition was changed from (size > arr.length * 2) to (size + 1 > array.length * 2), which affected whether a ConcurrentModificationException was thrown during internal rehashing. The test stabilized by run 22 once the rehash logic no longer triggered version increments visible to active iterators.
nextSteps: The modCount/expectedModCount pattern for fail-fast iterators recurs in every mutable collection you will write, including EditorTrees and graph structures. The key rule: increment the version counter exactly once per user-facing mutation (add, remove, clear), and never during internal operations like rehashing that do not change the logical contents of the set.

When implementing hasNext and next for a hash table iterator, maintain two pieces of state: the current bucket index and the current node within that bucket's chain. hasNext must scan forward through empty buckets to find the next non-null entry, not just compare an index to array.length.
Test your iterator by interleaving add/remove calls with iteration to verify that ConcurrentModificationException fires at the right times, and that internal rehashing does not falsely trigger it.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent rehash failures across multiple error types
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across all 21 runs before passing at run 22. The error progression moved through several distinct phases: NullPointerException and incorrect return values (runs 1-2), ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from negative hash indices (runs 3-7), assertion failures from incorrect bucket contents (runs 8-16), StackOverflowError likely from recursive rehashing (runs 17-18), and further ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and ConcurrentModificationException from rehash interactions (runs 19-21). The critical fix at run 22 changed stringHashIndex to accept a capacity parameter (stringHashIndex(String item, int max)) so that during rehashing, items could be re-indexed against the new array length rather than the old one. The rehash threshold was also corrected to (size + 1 > array.length * 2), checking the post-add size before actually adding. Additionally, the ordering was fixed so that size++ occurs before the hash index computation during rehash redistribution, and the rehash helper uses the passed-in array length rather than the instance field.
nextSteps: This rehash logic, where you double capacity and redistribute all existing items into new buckets, appears directly on Exam 3 (rehash diagram problem) and the Final Exam (amortized cost discussion). The core algorithm is: allocate a new array of double the length, iterate over every node in every bucket of the old array, and recompute each item's bucket index using the NEW array's length, not the old one.

When rehashing, avoid calling your public add method to re-insert items, as that can re-trigger version increments, duplicate checks, or recursive rehashing. Instead, write a private helper that directly inserts a node at the head of the appropriate bucket in the new array.

Always compute the bucket index relative to the array you are inserting into. Parameterizing your hash index method with the array length (as you did in run 22) is the correct approach to ensure items land in valid buckets during redistribution.

drills.intro: Exam 3 Problem 4(c) asks you to reason about *when* a capacity-doubling rehash happens given M and λ. To make that reasoning testable on your own implementation, add a new method `public int rehashCount()` to StringHashSet that returns how many rehashes have occurred since construction. You'll need a private instance field that you increment exactly once each time your resize/rehash branch runs. Then paste this test into StringHashSetTest.java for a point back. hints: Add a private int field initialized to 0 — e.g. `private int mRehashCount = 0;` — and a one-line public getter that returns it. The field tracks lifetime rehash count, not the count since the last clear().

Increment the field inside the branch that actually grows the array (your resize / rehash helper). Don't increment on every add() — only on the adds that crossed the lambda threshold and triggered a grow.

If the second assertion fails with a count of 0, your resize branch isn't running on the 11th add — re-read your threshold check. If it fails with 2, you may be calling resize from inside resize (e.g. recursive add during re-bucketing) — re-bucket directly into the new array instead of going through add().

feedbackItems.pattern: Missing duplicate detection in add
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed for 14 runs before passing at run 15. Early failures (runs 1-5) were caused by ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from negative hash indices. Once the index computation was stabilized around run 7, the test continued to fail because the add method did not check whether the item already existed in the bucket's chain before inserting a new node. The run 15 diff shows 26 lines added and 12 removed, which included adding the contains-check logic within add (walking the chain at the computed bucket to see if any node's data matches the item) and restructuring addAll to delegate properly. The diff also shows refinements to the iterator's hasNext/next traversal and the stringHashIndex helper. The duplicate detection fix was the key change: before inserting at the head of a bucket's chain, the add method must first traverse the existing chain and return false if the item is found.
nextSteps: In a set implementation, add must enforce uniqueness. The correct pattern for separate chaining is: compute the bucket index, walk the linked list at that bucket comparing each node's data to the new item (using .equals()), and only insert a new head node if no match is found. This same per-bucket walk is what Exam 3 tests when asking about collided entries.

Return a boolean from add: true if the item was actually inserted, false if it was a duplicate. This return value is what the test asserts on, and it also determines whether size should be incremented.
Consider extracting the chain-walk into a private helper (e.g., findInBucket) that both add and contains can call, reducing code duplication and ensuring consistent equality checks.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect return value from size() and cascading failures across core operations
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testAddAndRawStringNoCollision, testToString, testAddDuplicate, testAddAll, testClear, testRemove, and testContains, failed from run 1 through run 14 due to interconnected bugs in the core hash set operations. The size() method returned -1 (a placeholder) instead of the actual size field, and isEmpty() did not correctly check whether size was zero. At run 15, the code was updated to return this.size from size() and to use Arrays.asList(table).isEmpty() for isEmpty(), and the toString method was rewritten to walk chains using a while loop over each bucket rather than just printing the first node. These fixes resolved the immediate failures for this group of tests. However, subsequent runs introduced regressions: at run 26, the add() method was changed to link new nodes to table[pos+1] instead of table[pos], breaking separate chaining by connecting nodes across different buckets. Run 27 attempted to fix this with a bounds-checked next index, but the fundamental error of linking to the wrong bucket persisted. At run 62, the hash position calculation was changed from Math.floorMod(stringHashCode(item), capacity) to capacity % stringHashCode(item), which reverses the operands of the modulus and produces incorrect bucket indices. Run 64 corrected the operand order to stringHashCode(item) % capacity with a manual negative-check, which restored correct behavior. The position calculation was modified multiple times across runs 26, 27, 62, and 64.
nextSteps: Solidify your understanding of separate chaining: when inserting a new node, it must link to the existing head of the same bucket (table[pos]), not to an adjacent bucket. The new node becomes the new head: table[pos] = new Node(item, table[pos]).

For mapping hash codes to bucket indices, use Math.floorMod(hashCode, capacity) rather than manual modulus with negative correction. floorMod always returns a non-negative result when the divisor is positive, eliminating an entire class of bugs.

When multiple tests fail simultaneously, identify the shared dependency (here, add() and position calculation) rather than fixing each test individually. Tracing one add() call by hand through the bucket array can reveal whether nodes land in the correct chain.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent eager iterator in AdjacencyMatrix for both directions
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testPredecessorIteratorIsLazy and testSuccessorIteratorIsLazy for AdjacencyMatrix have been failing since run 8 and remain failing through run 35. The lazy iteration tests measure whether the iterator's constructor and first call to next() complete in O(1)-ish time, rather than eagerly building a full Set of neighbors. The AdjacencyList code diffs show the iterator implementations use the pattern `successorSet(key).iterator()` and `predecessorSet(key).iterator()`, which constructs the entire neighbor set before returning an iterator over it. This same eager approach appears in the AdjacencyMatrix implementation. For an adjacency matrix, building a successor or predecessor set requires scanning an entire row or column of the boolean matrix, which is O(n). The lazy iteration test expects that the constructor does minimal work (just recording the starting position) and that next() scans forward only until it finds the next true entry in the row/column, then stops. This blocker appears identically in both AdjacencyList and AdjacencyMatrix, indicating the iterator implementations pre-compute results rather than deferring computation to hasNext()/next() calls.
nextSteps: This lazy-iterator pattern recurs on the Final practice computer part, where successorIterator is called inside an inner loop and an eager implementation will time out. To fix it: write a custom inner class implementing Iterator<T> that stores a cursor (the current index into the matrix row or column). The constructor should only initialize the cursor and advance it to the first true entry. Each call to next() returns the element at the cursor and advances to the next true entry. hasNext() simply checks whether the cursor is still in bounds.

For AdjacencyMatrix specifically, successorIterator for vertex i should scan row i of the boolean[][] lazily: maintain an int field `nextIndex` starting at 0, and in the constructor (or a private advance() helper), increment nextIndex until matrix[i][nextIndex] is true or nextIndex reaches the array length. Each next() call saves the current nextIndex, advances past it, and returns the corresponding key.

Verify that your iterator throws NoSuchElementException from next() when hasNext() is false, completing the java.util.Iterator contract. This same pattern applies to every iterator you write in this course, including hash sets and EditorTrees.

hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testAddAndRawStringNoRehash(), failed from run 1 through run 14, requiring 15 total failing runs before passing in run 15. The core issue involved how elements were ordered within their chains during rehashing and insertion. The code diffs across runs 15, 16, and 17 all show changes in the add() method, specifically around the rehash trigger condition and the ordering of operations (checking contains before rehashing, ensuring rehash happens before insertion). The run 15 fix involved restructuring the add method and, critically, fixing the rehash logic so that when items are redistributed into a doubled-capacity table, they land in the correct buckets with the correct chain ordering. A regression in run 16 (with 26 lines changed) caused the test to fail again, but run 17 restored the correct behavior with a nearly identical diff to run 15. nextSteps: This load-factor threshold arithmetic recurs on Exam 3, where you must calculate how many adds trigger a rehash for a given capacity and lambda. Practice computing the threshold manually: with capacity M and max load factor lambda, rehash triggers when size + 1 > lambda * M, and verify your code matches that formula.

When implementing rehash, walk through the redistribution by hand: for each node in the old table, recompute its bucket index using (hashCode % newCapacity), and prepend it to the new chain. Verify that you are not reversing or losing nodes by reusing node references incorrectly.

All three tests share the same underlying code change and root cause. The remove() method was present in earlier runs but had bugs; the diff at run 24 shows significant restructuring (17 lines removed, 47 added), including changes to how compareTo was invoked (switching from raw casts to bounded type parameters), corrections to the recursive remove logic, and fixes to the return-value tracking via BooleanContainer. The before-state shows that insert() calls were appearing inside the remove helper (lines like `left = left.insert(i, b)` and `right = right.insert(i, b)` in the remove context), indicating the remove method's recursive calls were delegating to insert rather than to remove. The run 24 fix corrected the three-case removal logic (leaf node, one child, two children with in-order successor replacement) and ensured the boolean return value accurately reflected whether an element was actually removed. This three-case removal pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) applies the same leaf/one-child/two-children logic but adds AVL rebalancing on the way back up the recursion.
nextSteps: Solidify your understanding of the three-case BST removal algorithm, as it reappears in EditorTrees Milestone 3 with the added complexity of AVL rebalancing after deletion. Practice tracing removal of a two-child node: find the in-order successor (leftmost node in the right subtree), copy its data into the current node, then recursively remove the successor from the right subtree.

Pay close attention to the pointer-replacement pattern: each recursive call to remove() must return the (possibly updated) node reference so the parent can re-link its child. Returning NULL_NODE for a leaf deletion, returning the single child for a one-child case, and returning `this` (with swapped data) for the two-child case are the three distinct return paths.

When using a BooleanContainer or similar wrapper to track whether a mutation actually occurred, make sure the flag is set to true only when the target element is found and removed, not when the recursion simply traverses without finding it.

Uses the same one-child pointer-swap pattern as remove(), and the same return-value propagation pattern required for EditorTrees Milestone 3 deletion. hints: The minimum is always the leftmost node; keep following left pointers until you find a node whose left child is NULL_NODE.
Once found, unlink the minimum by replacing it with its right child (which may be NULL_NODE), exactly the same pointer-swap as removing a node with zero or one child in remove().
Return the data value from the removed node. In the recursive helper, when node.left == NULL_NODE, set the parent's left pointer to node.right and return node.data.

feedbackItems.pattern: Sustained failure in BST remove logic across multiple runs
feedbackItems.explanation: This test shares the same root cause and fix as testRemove() and testRemoveReturnValue(), all three passing together at run 24. testRemoveAdvanced() likely exercises more complex removal scenarios such as removing internal nodes with two children, removing the root, or performing multiple sequential removals. The code diff at run 24 reveals that the remove helper had been incorrectly calling insert() for its recursive subtree traversal, meaning the method was not descending to find and remove the target node. The fix restructured the remove logic with proper recursive calls and correct handling of all three removal cases. The bounded type parameter change (`T extends Comparable<T>`) also eliminated unsafe casts that could have caused subtle comparison issues.
nextSteps: For advanced removal scenarios (removing the root, removing nodes that cause cascading restructuring), trace through your algorithm on paper with a tree of at least 5-7 nodes. Verify that after each removal, the BST property holds for every node and the tree structure is correct.

The two-children case is the most error-prone: ensure you find the in-order successor correctly (go right once, then left as far as possible), copy only the data, and then remove the successor node from the right subtree. A common bug is forgetting to recursively remove the successor after copying its value.

Test your remove() with sequences that hit all three cases in succession, for example: remove a leaf, then remove a node with one child, then remove a node with two children, checking the tree's toString() or toArrayList() output after each step.

feedbackItems.pattern: Sustained failure in BST remove return-value logic
feedbackItems.explanation: This test validates that remove() returns the correct boolean: true when an element was found and removed, false when the element was not present. It shares the same fix point (run 24) and code changes as testRemove() and testRemoveAdvanced(). The BooleanContainer pattern used to propagate the success/failure result from the recursive helper back to the public remove() method was not functioning correctly before run 24, likely because the recursive calls were invoking insert() instead of remove(), so the container's value was never being set to true upon finding the target. The run 24 fix corrected the recursive delegation and ensured the BooleanContainer flag was set appropriately when the target node was located and removed.
nextSteps: The return-value wrapper pattern (BooleanContainer) is a common technique when a recursive method needs to return a modified node reference AND a success/failure indicator. Make sure you understand why a simple boolean return is insufficient here: the recursive helper must return the updated Node pointer, so the boolean must travel through a separate channel.

When the element is not found (recursion reaches NULL_NODE without matching), the BooleanContainer should remain false. When the element is found and removed, set it to true at the exact point of removal, not during traversal. This distinction is critical for correctness.

This same pattern of returning a node while communicating side information through a wrapper object appears in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where deletion must also communicate balance-factor changes up the call stack.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 1
episodeSummaries.summary: The student began with working size() and height() methods, then encountered a catastrophic compilation crisis where core method signatures (insert, contains, remove, isEmpty, iterators, toArray, toArrayList) became undefined. Multiple runs showed no code changes as the student appeared stuck, unable to resolve the compilation errors. By the end of the episode, the student restored height() and size() manual tests but the core methods remained unimplemented.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 2
episodeSummaries.summary: A single stagnation run with no code changes. All 22 tests continued failing due to missing method signatures. The student appeared to be reviewing the codebase without making modifications.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 3
episodeSummaries.summary: Major breakthrough: the student implemented the insert() method with proper null-checking and exception handling, passing 6 new tests and unlocking the insert, edge_cases, and efficiency categories. The student also implemented contains(), passing testContainsInts(). However, a toString() representation bug emerged, blocking several tests that relied on string output.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 4
episodeSummaries.summary: A single verification run with no code changes. The student paused after implementing insert() and contains(), likely analyzing the toString() bug and planning next steps.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 5
episodeSummaries.summary: The student implemented the isEmpty() method, unlocking the isEmpty test category. This was an incremental addition to the growing set of working BST operations.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 6
episodeSummaries.summary: The student implemented toArrayList() and toArray() methods, unlocking both test categories with 3 new tests passing. This demonstrated understanding of in-order tree traversal for collection conversion.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 7
episodeSummaries.summary: The student implemented the inefficientIterator() method, unlocking that test category. The toString() bug persisted but the student continued building out iterator functionality.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 8
episodeSummaries.summary: The student implemented the preOrderIterator() method, unlocking the preOrderIterator test category. Remove tests were now compiling but failing on logic, indicating the method stub existed but had incorrect behavior.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 9
episodeSummaries.summary: The student implemented the in-order iterator() method, completing all three iterator variants. Then they fixed the critical toString() bug that had been blocking 4 tests across multiple categories (insert, contains, toString). After this fix, the student entered a prolonged stall of 6 runs with no code changes, appearing stuck on the remove() algorithm.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 10
episodeSummaries.summary: After the extended stall, the student finally implemented remove() logic and then debugged it to handle all cases correctly—fixing inverted return values and the three-child node removal case. All 3 remove tests passed, unlocking the remove category. This was the final major feature implementation.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 11
episodeSummaries.summary: A regression was introduced where the insert() method's null-checking was accidentally broken, causing testInsertExceptions to fail. The student quickly identified and fixed the issue, restoring 100% test passage.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 12
episodeSummaries.summary: A verification run with all 24 tests passing. The student confirmed stability of the codebase after the previous regression fix.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 13
episodeSummaries.summary: A second regression cycle: the student modified the remove() method and accidentally broke its null-checking exception handling. testRemoveIllegalArgumentException failed. The student then fixed the issue in a subsequent run, restoring all tests to passing.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 14
episodeSummaries.summary: Final verification run confirming all 24 tests pass. The student appears to be validating the stability of the complete BST implementation after the second regression fix.

episodeSummaries.label: Episode 15
